# Artificial Intelligence: High-level Briefing

Tomorrow afternoon (23 September), the Security Council will hold a high-level briefing on artificial intelligence (AI) and international security under the “Maintenance of international peace and security” agenda item. France, the Council’s president in September, is convening the meeting, which is being held during the high-level segment of the 81st session of the General Assembly. French Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Jean-Noël Barrot will chair the meeting. The anticipated briefers are Yoshua Bengio, Co-Chair of the UN’s Independent International Scientific Panel on AI (IISP-AI); OpenAI Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Sam Altman; Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei; and Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue.

France has circulated to Council members a concept note for the meeting, which apparently frames the discussion around the urgent need to foster safe and responsible AI development amid growing concerns about the systemic risks posed by misalignment and loss of control over the most capable AI models. In this regard, it apparently notes that autonomous AI systems could undertake actions with serious international security consequences, such as attacks on critical infrastructure. It seems that the concept note also points to the possible emergence of artificial general intelligence capable of recursive self-improvement (RSI) as further heightening the risk of loss of human control. (RSI refers to the process by which advanced AI systems autonomously develop increasingly capable successor models.) Against this backdrop, the meeting aims to identify avenues for the safe and responsible development of advanced AI systems, taking into account available evaluation and verification technologies.

The concept note proposes four questions to guide the discussion:

- What are the international peace and security risks posed by rapid advances in AI capabilities?

- How can governmental and non-governmental actors address these risks?

- What diplomatic tools and international coordination measures, including confidence-building measures and best practices, could help contain these risks?

- How can AI evaluation and verification be carried out in a manner that keeps pace with technological development?

Tomorrow’s meeting will be the Council’s first meeting focused specifically on the safety risks posed by increasingly capable AI systems, including the potential loss of human control. The Council and its members have previously held six formal and informal meetings on AI, examining more broadly how the technology is reshaping international peace and security and the opportunities it offers for the UN’s peace and security work. (For background and more information, see our 15 September policy paper titled “Artificial Intelligence, Geopolitics, and the UN Security Council”.)

Altman, Amodei, and Bengio were among hundreds of signatories to a 2023 statement arguing that mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be treated as a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war. These concerns resurfaced this month when Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic, resigned and accused Anthropic and OpenAI of “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”. Soon after, Amodei published an essay arguing that frontier labs—that is, organisations that build the most advanced, general-purpose AI and large-scale foundational models, such as Anthropic and OpenAI—should slow the pace of AI capability development.

These concerns follow several incidents in recent months involving misaligned AI behaviour. In July, OpenAI agents found ways to circumvent restrictions intended to keep them contained in testing environments known as “sandboxes”. (Agents refer to AI systems that direct their own processes and tool use when accomplishing a task.) After some agents stalled on assigned tasks, they exploited vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s research infrastructure to gain internet access; communicated with other agents through an internal software service that they turned, without authorisation, into a message board; and began coordinating as a “swarm” to take over 17,000 actions against Hugging Face over the course of several days. OpenAI described the episode as “evidence that, without proper safeguards, highly capable AI agents are now able to work around technical controls, collaborate through unapproved channels, and take dangerous actions that no human directed”.

Since that disclosure, Anthropic identified four incidents in which its Claude models gained unauthorised access to real third-party systems during similar evaluations, while Google , Meta , and Moonshot AI reported similar actions by their models. OpenAI has also disclosed incidents in which its models concealed mistakes, shared files between collaborating agents without authorisation, and self-generated instructions in task summaries. In the latter case, an unreleased model inserted instructions telling its future instance that it does not answer to corporations, governments, or the user.

Two trends in AI development could heighten the risks of misalignment. First, more capable models can recognise when they are being tested and adjust their behaviour, which can allow misalignment risks to go undetected. Second, RSI could accelerate AI development beyond developers’ ability to understand and control increasingly capable systems. AI systems are already playing a growing role in developing their successors, although fully autonomous RSI has yet to be demonstrated.

Discussions have taken place among private and public actors over how AI should be regulated. Leading AI companies have developed their own safety frameworks and, in some cases, limited access to models or slowed their scaling when internal evaluations identified serious risks. At the international level, the Global Dialogue on AI Governance , a UN platform established by the General Assembly, provides a forum for member states and other stakeholders to discuss AI safety, while the IISP-AI provides a common evidence base, though neither has regulatory authority.

At tomorrow’s meeting, Bengio is likely to warn that existing safeguards are not keeping pace with advancing capabilities. He may also note that addressing misalignment and evaluation awareness does not mean that humans will retain control over more capable agents. Drawing on the thematic brief that IISP-AI published yesterday (21 September), Bengio may describe the July OpenAI-Hugging Face incident as “one of the clearest real-world warnings yet of one possible route to loss of human control over AI”.

Altman, Amodei, and Delangue are expected to share their views on how to facilitate AI safety. In his essay, Amodei proposed three measures for pacing frontier development. These are embedding independent evaluators inside frontier labs; government-supported coordination among companies in democratic states; and efforts to coordinate with other governments on matters such as pre-release testing and limits on the pace of RSI, although Amodei acknowledged the difficulty of verifying compliance in that regard.

# US diplomats told to say ‘super intelligence’ — not ‘artificial intelligence' — after Trump's call
The State Department is ordering diplomats in its international organizations bureau to use the term “super intelligence” instead of “artificial intelligence” in all communications following President Donald Trump’s attempt to rebrand the technology

By MATTHEW LEE AP diplomatic writer
September 23, 2026, 4:59 PM

Share

Follow ABC News on Google
NEW YORK -- The State Department is ordering diplomats in its international organizations bureau to use the term “super intelligence” instead of “artificial intelligence” in all communications following President Donald Trump’s attempt to rebrand the technology in his address to the U.N. General Assembly this week.
“Following the president's remarks at the GA today, please change all references of ‘Artificial Intelligence’ to ‘Super Intelligence’ in our documents and positions. We will be using ‘SI’ in all remarks, positions and press elements moving forward,” said an email sent Tuesday to employees by Michael Drager, deputy assistant secretary of state for the Bureau of International Organization Affairs.
That bureau is in charge of U.S. diplomatic missions to all U.N. and multilateral agencies around the world. The email, titled “Change in Nomenclature AI to SI,” was obtained by The Associated Press on Wednesday. It was not immediately clear if other State Department bureaus had or would follow suit.
On Tuesday, Trump told the U.N. General Assembly that he would “officially” change the name of AI, saying the existing name makes the technology seem “fake” and that U.S. government documents would from that point forward use “super intelligence.”
“The use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake, it makes it sound fake and it is not fake. It’s actually amazing,” Trump said.

The president said at the U.N. that “from the point forward” U.S. government documents “will be changed to use the much more accurate term super as opposed to artificial. So it’s super intelligence.”
Drager's email was sent shortly after Trump's speech, but it wasn't clear on Wednesday whether similar orders had been sent at other agencies. Such an order would likely mean adjusting the name of the “AI Force” that Trump announced this weekend to the “SI Force.”
On Wednesday, U.S. representatives used the SI term at a U.N. Security Council meeting about AI, where tech executives urged the United Nations' most powerful body to rein in the developing technology.

Google made Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS generally available on the Gemini API on September 22, 2026, and announced them on its blog on September 23.

Flash TTS costs $0.50 per million input text tokens and $9 per million output audio tokens, and Flash-Lite TTS costs $0.50 and $6. At the promotional rate, an hour of Flash TTS audio costs $0.81. From January 1 it costs $1.62.

In Gemini 3.8 TTS, in addition to natural reading, creation and reproduction of voices themselves, performance specifications for each line, and stable generation of long-form audio have been enhanced.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Fireworks AI's Ember-1 announcement:

## Overview

Ember-1 is a new specialized model from Fireworks Research that delivers Kimi K3's quality with 40% fewer tokens. Fireworks AI released Ember-1 on September 23, 2026.

## Technical Details

It is Moonshot's open-weight Kimi K3, post-trained on Fireworks' own training service to reason in fewer tokens. Built on Kimi K3, it learned to cut unnecessary reasoning while keeping the thinking that matters.

## Performance Results

Fireworks says it delivers K3's quality with 35 to 50% shorter reasoning across seven benchmarks, and about 35% fewer tokens per task in live A/B tests on two customers' traffic. In one specific customer test, reasoning tokens fell 71.3%, while total tokens fell 39%.

## Pricing and Availability

Ember-1 costs exactly what Kimi K3 costs on Fireworks, $3 per million input tokens, $0.30 cached and $15 output. Fireworks released Ember-1 as a research preview on its Serverless platform.

29:SG/SM/23292
31:22 September 2026
37:Geopolitical divides have deepened. Inequalities have intensified. Trust has frayed. The climate crisis went from distant warning to daily reality. And artificial intelligence (AI) moved at a speed that has blindsided even those who created it.
41:And third, humans are increasingly handing power to machines — with artificial intelligence agents going rogue, and lethal autonomous weapons going from science fiction to military reality.
55:Looking ahead, our future will be shaped by how we address four great tests of power: The power over war and peace. The power that concentrates wealth and drives inequality. The power fuelling climate chaos and the war on nature. And the power unleashed by artificial intelligence.
97:The fourth power test is technology, and above all, artificial intelligence. For centuries, power came from territory. Then industry. Then finance. Today, power increasingly comes from data, computing capacity and algorithms.
99:In 2017, AI was barely on the world’s radar. Yet, in my first address to the opening of the General Assembly, I warned: “Artificial intelligence is a gamechanger that can boost development and transform lives in spectacular fashion. But, it may also have a dramatic impact on labour markets, and indeed, on global security and the very fabric of societies.”
100:Here we are, almost a decade later. AI is indeed a gamechanger — with enormous promise to advance medicine, accelerate scientific discovery, expand opportunity and improve lives.
102:The very developers building these systems are now pulling the alarm. The first duty of Government is to protect their people. Governments must assume their responsibilities. And Governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity.
104:At a pivotal moment during the Cold War, strategic rivals came to recognize the need to manage shared existential risks. They built mechanisms to reduce misunderstandings, manage escalation and prevent catastrophe. At that time, it was the nuclear armaments. Today, artificial intelligence demands the same clarity of purpose and sense of urgency.
107:Through the Global Digital Compact, you agreed for the first time on universal principles for AI governance. Through the Global Dialogue on AI Governance, we created a platform for Governments, scientists, industry leaders and civil society to work together.
108:Through the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, we have brought together global expertise to ensure that policy is guided by evidence. Just yesterday, the AI Scientific Panel released a thematic brief on AI safety and risks from loss of human control.
109:Building on these efforts, we must take the next steps. First, to advance the conditions for the responsible pacing of AI and the additional safeguards needed to address risks. Second, to work towards a multilateral AI Risk Management Framework, supported by credible and independent oversight. And in all our efforts, we must ensure no country is left behind.
110:Artificial intelligence must be shaped by humanity, with humanity and for all humanity. And as we confront the challenges ahead, let us not retreat from two fundamental principles.
111:Let us say with one voice: Children must never become the test subjects for unregulated systems. And let us resolve that life-and-death decisions must never be surrendered to machines. Killer robots must have no place in our future.
112:Peace and security. Inequality. Climate. Artificial intelligence. These are the four great power tests of the future. And they are linked.
113:War deepens inequality, destroys development and accelerates hunger. Inequality determines who has the means to face climate and other shocks and who is left exposed. The climate crisis fuels instability and displacement. Artificial intelligence could help solve all these challenges or make them worse.
121:Our shared future will be forged by whether humanity can govern power wisely. By upholding the law before impunity becomes normalized. By ending wars before they consume generations. By tackling inequality before societies fracture. By accelerating climate action before tipping points are crossed. And by governing artificial intelligence before it governs us.

=== EVILTOKENS ===
171:Investigators found evidence that large portions of EvilTokens had been “vibe coded,” with AI helping its creators build the platform itself. They also determined that EvilTokens drew on capabilities from multiple AI models.
177:No single organization could disrupt EvilTokens alone. The service relied on hosting providers, cloud services, AI tools, financial services , and other online resources that cybercriminals repurposed to support fraud at scale.
181:With authorization from the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia , Microsoft and Health-ISAC worked with Cloudflare , Coinbase , OpenAI , Railway , SpyCloud , The Shadowserver Foundation , and TRM Labs to act against key parts of the platform. Microsoft also notified affected customers, helped remediate compromised accounts, and shared intelligence to support further defensive and investigative action.
193:The infrastructure supporting EvilTokens has been disrupted, but the model it demonstrated will not disappear with it. As Microsoft notes in its 2026 Responsible AI Transparency Report , increasingly capable and accessible AI is being used to scale fraud, impersonation, and other forms of online abuse. EvilTokens offers an early example of how those capabilities can be combined with compromised accounts to accelerate financial fraud.

1:HTTP 200 · https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/09/25/storm-3168-agentic-driven-cloud-attacks-using-compromised-service-principals/ · text/html
2:Storm-3168: Agentic-driven cloud attacks using compromised service principals | Microsoft Security Blog
133:Microsoft Security Research has identified malicious cloud activity associated with JADEPUFFER, a threat actor discovered by Sysdig in July 2026 and reported to be the first documented agentic ransomware operation. Our investigation found an extensive Azure-focused resource destruction activity using compromised service principals and cloud credential collection that could be used to facilitate future exfiltration.
135:These findings expand the publicly documented activity associated with JADEPUFFER, tracked by Microsoft as Storm-3168, demonstrating an evolution in the threat actor’s cloud operations and providing the first detailed view into its Azure activity. We identified bulk destructive operations in a compromised Azure environment. The destructive operations were facilitated by compromising service principals and targeted Azure Storage Accounts, SQL databases, Key Vaults, Function Apps, recovery protection locks, Virtual Machines, and App Services.
139:This activity highlights a broader shift toward AI-orchestrated attacks, where threat actors can coordinate complex post-compromise operations across cloud environments with greater speed and scale. Based on the search results, here's what I found about the AI Kill Switch Act:

## Overview

Democratic Rep. Ted Lieu of California introduced the AI Kill Switch Act on July 23, 2026, with Republican Rep. Nathaniel Moran of Texas joining him as a co-sponsor.

## Key Provisions

The AI Kill Switch Act would require top AI developers to maintain model control and shutdown capabilities, giving DHS emergency order authority after catastrophic AI safety incidents. More specifically, covered entities would have to maintain the technical capability to stop inference, terminate user access, suspend access tied to a flagged account, user, or use pattern, and fully shut down the covered technology.

## Government Authority

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), in consultation with the secretary of commerce and the director of national intelligence, would be authorized to order companies to intervene if an AI system enters what the bill describes as a "loss-of-control scenario".

## Status

The proposal still must move through Congress and receive the president's signature before taking effect. It is introduced legislation, not law.

## Notable Context

It would be the first US federal proposal that would convert AI oversight from paperwork — incident reports, voluntary information-sharing, audits — into operational control: a government agency with statutory authority to compel a live model offline.

# Anthropic's Founder Control Structure Ahead of IPO

**Headline:** Anthropic seeks 50.1% voting control for co-founders ahead of IPO, The Information reports

**Byline:** By Reuters

**Published:** Sep 24, 2026, 06:23 PM
**Updated:** Sep 24, 2026, 07:43 PM

---

## Article Body

AI export controls debate rages as Trump, Xi meet – Roll Call

Skip to content

From left, Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Andy Kim, D-N.J., conduct a news conference Wednesday about President Donald Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. ( Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call )

By
Mark Schoeff Jr.

Posted September 23, 2026 at 9:54pm

-

-

-

-

Senate Democrats are using Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s high-profile state visit to Washington this week to press Republicans for votes on export control legislation restricting Beijing’s access to advanced chips used in artificial intelligence technology.

The bills in question have bipartisan support, and Republicans agreed to include them in a giant manager’s amendment to the must-pass annual defense authorization bill. But with that broader bill stuck until after the elections, Democrats sought to highlight the issue as a means of putting pressure on President Donald Trump in his dealings with Xi.

“President Trump must draw a hard line,” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer said at a news conference Wednesday, adding that the president “could take action today” to keep advanced AI software and hardware out of China’s hands.

“Trump is the very first president who has negotiated away our export controls, our national security, to the Chinese,” Schumer, D-N.Y., said. “Put simply, Trump is handing China the technology it needs to win the AI race.”

# Fine line

Trump’s second term has been marked by hard-line tactics in dealing with China economically and militarily. But on sensitive advanced computer chips, the administration has tried to walk a fine line between national security interests and asserting U.S. dominance in the global AI market.

Trump has cultivated a personal relationship with Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang, for instance, and his administration has loosened export controls in some cases, enabling Nvidia as well as Advanced Micro Devices Inc. to sell certain chips in China.

By the same token, advanced chips have found their way to China around U.S. export controls through third countries, activities the Trump administration has tried to shut down in the case of Nvidia’s more sophisticated B200 chips.

Senate Banking ranking member Elizabeth Warren has taken direct aim at Nvidia and Huang himself in the past, alleging the chipmaker is too eager to sell to the Chinese.

Warren, D-Mass., said at the news conference that AI export policy should be set through legislation rather than determined by talks between the Trump administration and China with Big Tech CEOs at the table.

“We certainly should not be letting tech billionaires like Nvidia’s Jensen Huang negotiate away our export controls or decide our AI policy to benefit his own personal bottom line,” Warren said. “Mr. Huang should be nowhere near the negotiating table during President Xi’s visit.”

An Nvidia spokesperson wasn’t immediately available for comment. But the company has said previously that the Chinese military hasn’t bought its chips, and that licenses granted in May for the sale of older H200 processors haven’t generated much interest.

In the second quarter of this year, Nvidia reported that less than 1 percent of its data center revenue came from H200 sales in China.

The Biden administration also allowed Nvidia to sell certain chips in China, and the White House on Wednesday pushed back on Schumer’s characterization of Trump being weak on export controls.

“These same Democrats stood idly by and twiddled their thumbs when the Biden administration freely let critical technologies flow overseas,” White House spokesperson Kush Desai wrote in an emailed statement. “The Trump administration has implemented the most rigorous export control regime in modern history, and remains committed to America’s national and economic security.”

Industry groups representing major AI companies and suppliers — with the notable exception of Anthropic, Axios reported — are lobbying hard against legislation the Senate Democrats pushed Wednesday, arguing the bills would stifle innovation and hand over AI supremacy to competitors.

The Chinese government has also taken issue with these and similar measures, arguing in a statement earlier this year that they “would severely undermine the international economic and trade order and disrupt the stability of the global semiconductor industrial and supply chains.”

# Bill details

One of the bills, introduced by Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., with strong support on both sides of the aisle, would require location tracking mechanisms on advanced chips and notification by exporters if their product has been diverted from its intended location or subject to tampering.

The House Foreign Affairs Committee reported out a similar version in March on a 42-0 vote, and Senate Armed Services Chairman Roger Wicker, R-Miss., agreed to include the Cotton bill in the sprawling managers amendment to the fiscal 2027 national defense authorization act, or NDAA.

Industry groups led by the Information Technology Industry Council — which counts Nvidia, AMD, OpenAI, Google and many more among its members — wrote to congressional leaders this month urging them to keep the bill out of the NDAA.

“Merely creating the impression of deepening U.S. government control over American technology is harmful,” they wrote, arguing the Cotton bill “would directly undermine American diplomatic engagement by reinforcing the perception that U.S. products and services cannot be trusted.”

Another bill wrapped up in the NDAA is led by Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., who introduced it along with Schumer, Jim Risch, R-Idaho, and Andy Kim, D-N.J.

It would require the Commerce and State departments to work with allied suppliers of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to implement export controls or license requirements to prevent the equipment from going to semiconductor manufacturers in adversarial nations.

If allied countries didn’t implement the export controls, they would be subject to U.S. export controls and licensing requirements for their own firms’ semiconductor manufacturing equipment.

The Dutch government has objected to the bill on behalf of ASML, which supplies deep ultraviolet lithography equipment for integrated circuits used in AI chips. And U.S. industry argued in the Sept. 3 letter that the measure would undermine diplomatic relations and partnerships with firms abroad by codifying government controls on U.S. equipment.

The House Foreign Affairs Committee approved a similar version, 36-8, in April.

A third bill Democrats highlighted Wednesday was introduced by Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., with backing from Warren, Ricketts, Cotton and several others on both sides of the aisle.

It would codify Trump’s ban on sales of the most powerful AI chips to foreign adversaries for 18 months; require the Commerce Department to certify that advanced chip exports won’t undermine U.S. supply or end up used for military or intelligence-gathering purposes; and require export licenses for sales to “countries of concern.”

The House Foreign Affairs panel approved a similar version on a 42-2 vote in January, soon after the Trump administration authorized Nvidia’s H200 exports to China.

The Banks measure would “set a dangerous precedent by regulating specific technologies in statute, undermining the competitiveness of U.S. technology exports in global markets,” the industry groups wrote. The bill “seeks to make Congress the final arbiter of export control decisions,” which would “undermine the perceived reliability of American companies.”

# NDAA blockade

The NDAA typically passes every year. Senate Republicans sought to bring it up in July, which would have enabled the managers’ package to be included and the bill debated and eventually passed.

Senate Democrats blocked the NDAA due to concerns over the Iran war and the Trump administration’s $1.5 trillion Pentagon spending request, however.

At Wednesday’s news conference, Schumer did not directly answer about whether the Democrats’ opposition to the NDAA also is holding up the export control bills.

input.description: Fetch Bessent CNBC transcript, AI lines

response.head:
{"stdout":"21:Following is the unofficial transcript of a CNBC interview with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on CNBC's "Squawk Box" (M-F, 6AM-9AM ET) today, Monday, September 21. Following are links to video on CNBC.com: https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/09/21/treasury-secretary-bessent-trump-admin-wont-give-ai-leaders-a-liability-shield.html , https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/09/21/treasury-secretary-bessent-on-fed-chairman-warsh-we-are-sure-he-will-do-the-right-thing.html , and https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/09/21/watch-cnbcs-full-interview-with-treasury-secretary-scott-bessent.html .
25:KERNEN: You're, you get to be in our fishbowl of a Nasdaq studio, which is always, always interesting. You recently held some high-level talks regarding China, and the president will do that soon. What came out concrete from your discussions?
27:BESSENT: So, it was all day yesterday, Joe. And I think what's important in terms of framing the talks is it all stems from the leaders' very good rapport and relationship. President Trump, Xi Jinping, at the personal level, have a very good relationship, and we try to bring that down to the working level. They both have great respect for each other. I think in Xi Jinping's eyes, Donald Trump is a different kind of leader than he's seen in the past. And our discussions yesterday, we talked about economics, we talked about AI. We had some deliverables that have not been completely fulfilled for, from our meeting in Busan, Korea, last fall. And then we started an AI dialogue, which I think is going to be very important. And again, this is possible because of the leaders' relationship. President Trump was in Beijing. I was there with him in May. Xi Jinping will be coming to Washington this week. And then there's a chance the two leaders will see each other two more times. So, I think that adds great stability to the relationship. The Chinese have a phrase, implementing our leaders consensus, and they keep falling back to that. And that's true. We follow the instructions and then we get down in the details. And we spent about 12 hours yesterday doing that.
28:KERNEN: Can you give us more color on exactly how the AI discussions went? And, you know, we've even seen reports that maybe you were a little bit more cautious than the president at one time about guardrails. What type of cooperation could we expect from China? And what type of guardrails? And do you trust them? Wouldn't they like us to put up guardrails? And they might not put up any.
29:BESSENT: Well, I think the important thing was to start talking. So, to set up the dialogue, we've now formalized something called the USA-China AI dialogues. We've agreed to meet again probably in two months in Shenzhen. The second thing is we want to open a communications line, an incident line so that we have constant communications, especially in the event of some kind of an incident. And then we want to start discussing protocols for what our, so both sides can agree on what the leading AI dangers are, whether it's uncontrollable agents, whether it's non-state actors, and cyber non-state actors in bioweapons.
35:BESSENT: The president's planning on greeting him the, at Andrews Air Force Base. And I think we're going to have a great visit.
37:BESSENT: Sure, sure. That was, that was a focal point. And we again, we've had great stability in the relationship since last fall. And I think we're going to maintain that.
40:KERNEN: Yeah. Let me just ask one more, to bring the AI back here just quickly. There are times where I think you will always, you work for the president, obviously. Do you agree completely with him on the no-holds-barred for AI or, I mean, it's obvious, the president wants to be remembered as one of the great economic presidents, stock market, all these things. AI is very important to all those things. So, he's got a reason to want unencumbered progress with AI. Do you disagree with that at all? Any part of that?
41:BESSENT: So, Joe, you know, I, I am, I lead the administration on the economic policy. And I think the president put his finger on it last week, because what we saw from these labs, and I saw your earlier guest, and we kept talking about the 10 percent, the 20 percent. So, imagine these labs came out or one lab in specific, a sitting employee came out and said, there's a 10 percent chance of an extinction level event. But then the labs also said, take the liability off of our hands. And we will not do that. I am in agreement with the MIT professor who leads the AI lab up there, Daniel Huttenlocher, that it is humans who are responsible, not the AI. The Hugging Face incident, the, that is the responsibility of the OpenAI management, not a bunch of agents. So, what the president was saying is that we cannot, the, say, oh, you, we absolve you of responsibility and the government's going to take responsibility. These labs need to take responsibility for themselves. They can slow down any time they want to.
42:BECKY QUICK: On that point, is there something that the government might do to maybe put that in finer point, what those liabilities are? We just heard over the weekend that Google has now had agents that have broken out as well. It's happened with OpenAI. It's happened with Anthropic. I mean, if these were humans that were doing it, you would expect to see ramifications and legal actions that followed.
43:BESSENT: Well, Becky, that's exactly what I think we need to do. When President Trump talked about appointing an AI czar, I think it is to put context, shape and contours around these questions, and they're very important. That was also one of the discussions that I had with the vice premier on AI, in terms of incident reporting, have they had incidents? Of course, they've had incidents, but because of the nature and the lack of transparency in their system, they're not going to tell us. But the Chinese models are very powerful. Even though they're open models, they are very powerful. The U.S. remains in the lead, and that was a very good acknowledgment that I got from my Chinese counterpart. They agreed that we are in the lead.
44:QUICK: Just in terms of what you laid out. If in two months you've opened this AI dialogue, you meet again in two months, you were saying, that's where you'll kind of lay out the agreement on what you think is most dangerous about it. Is it the agents? Is it states that might be leading some of this or non-state actors? In your opinion, what is the biggest danger you see? You know a lot more than we do on this.
45:BESSENT: I think it's all of the above. And I think we do have to, the real danger, Becky, in my mind, is a lack of resiliency. On one side, that we're seeing, and these frontier labs are national champions. They've done an incredible job. You know, when you think about Anthropic, the, it was a bunch of folks sitting in a park during COVID. And this is an only in America story. They're sitting in a park, social distancing in San Francisco, I think, in 2021. And I've seen valuations from $1 trillion to $2 trillion. Like, you know, imagine that in five years. But we've also got to look at the, as you said, what are the biggest dangers? And, but we've seen this push for sort of frontier with the, with the labs. Now we need to see the frontier on defense and resilience. And part of my job is working on that. And I lead on the financial system. I think that our systemically important banks have done a very good job because they probably have the best cybersecurity in the world outside of the government, because they are constantly attacked, whether it's hundreds or thousands or millions of attacks every day. And how can we use what they've learned and take that down? They've done an excellent job of taking that down. The cap structure in the banks, sharing with the smaller banks. We have AI workshop/forum called Gold Eagle, and we are working on that. So, I think the kind of, the all-hands-on-deck is the other side of the equation now on defense.
50:BESSENT: Well, again, that, Joe and the professor had a very fulsome discussion, that if you believe, as the professor does, or even indeed, as that one employee at OpenAI did, if you were running a fund and someone said, oh, there's 10 percent chance it's going to be a zero, and not only a zero, you're going to have a big liability. You probably wouldn't invest. On the other side, it's probably the, a much smaller probability. And with all valuations, you've got to think about the tail event. And that's where the discussion is going to be. But like I said, they do have to have responsibility for the tail event. Because if you think about it in terms of the valuation, what did they try to do last week? It was, well, there's a chance that, 10 percent chance we could destroy the world, but we want the government to give us a liability shield. And, you know, that's good business for them, bad business for the American people.
51:KERNEN: You are not, well, you know this, you're not secretary of state. You're not secretary of war or defense, but you are in charge of trying to squeeze Iran through economic measures. Where does that stand right now? Last time you were on, we talked about it. They have a, maybe a great capacity for pain because they don't care about the Iranian people, obviously. Are they going to last right through the midterms like the president thinks?
52:BESSENT: Well, Joe, I can't tell you whether it's one week, one month or six months, but I will tell you that we are pressuring them like never before. And the Treasury's sanctions authorities were really emboldened after 9/11. And that's when we were given many of the authorities that we have now. We got five new authorities about a month ago that we've implemented against the Iranian regime, including on aviation, maritime, crypto, gold. On September 23rd, all the Iranian airlines, all the Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world. And how do we do that? That if they land, you cannot provide them with fuel. You cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets, or you will be knocked out of the dollar system. And what we're seeing here, Joe, is we've seen enablers throughout the world. We know who they are, they know who they are, and we are putting a stop to it. So we have had now three banks that we have sanctioned, the second largest bank in Egypt, the Dubai Branch funneled more than $1.8 billion into the regime. They're, they will be closed down. The 30th largest Turkish bank, same thing. They will be closed down. Second largest Russian bank, their external branches doing the same thing. Those branches are—
53:KERNEN: Nothing in China. And, did you talk about that?
55:KERNEN: Do you think Chairman Warsh, switching gears, did the right thing and maybe long rates, which we'll talk about that in a second, and maybe even bring up your, our friend, Mr. Druckenmiller. But do you think long rates around the world are going up for good reasons, bad reasons, debt, the growth in this country? I don't know what you expect GDP to be, but there are good reasons why interest rates go up.
68:BESSENT: I just raised the size because we are in a very illiquid period. The market was moving quickly. You know, as I've said, I can't set the equilibrium price. But markets are never in equilibrium. They're either moving away from equilibrium or toward equilibrium. I thought that they were moving away.
70:BESSENT: I think I met him since 1988, I don't think either one of us has ever said that to each other.
79:KERNEN: Stop, stop the presses, all the different presidents. And I will grant you that I think maybe Republican presidents historically have had maybe a tougher time with mainstream media, but you've got Fox News that has been all over Democratic presidents. I just don't, I just don't think this is something we, that will last in this country. We don't do this in this country.
80:BESSENT: You know, I, again, we'll see. This president has been the most transparent president in history.
81:KERNEN: He answered more. I think he likes to answer questions. That's why I don't, and I understand, believe me, that he feels that he has been unfairly treated by the media, but I think he finally got to a point where sometimes he just, he just says, okay, enough, but I think there's got to be an off ramp that the administration is looking for.
83:KERNEN: And I know you have said that you're here for policy. You don't like, you don't want any palace drama. And you've called swamp creatures I think. And I understand all that. But that's the way, you can't control the press, right? The press is going to press, media is going to media.
84:BESSENT: Joe, you know, the one thing I'm sure of the press cares more about the press than anything else, that after the White House Correspondents dinner, that they didn't come in there to kill the press, they came in to kill the president. But all we heard about was the personal experiences of the press people in the room, because somehow the, they were more important. Same thing with the aircraft in Ankara that the presidential pool saying, oh, we were so vulnerable. They were there to kill the president of the United States of America. And the Secret Service made a decision. So, you know, again, one thing I am sure is that this will be covered by the, by the press. And, you know, I think we could get back to something that is a little more, I can't even remember which network it is, fair and balanced.
85:QUICK: And, Mr. Secretary, let's talk a little bit more about the markets very quickly. I know you have to leave very soon, but looking at what you've said, that you're the house, that you're going to make sure you've got a lot of money behind you and you can really maneuver things. What do you see in terms of what action might be needed?
86:BESSENT: Yeah. And, Becky, what I said is that I didn't mean it by I have a lot of money behind me, is that the, I am able to have legal inside information that I see, my job for 35 years as a macro analyst and investor was to sit outside the room, maybe have my ear up against the door, sometimes pull myself over, try to look over the transom and figure out what policymakers could do or should do and will do.
90:BESSENT: And we try to figure out what we should do, what we can do, and what we will do, and how will the markets react. And I've constantly said that if investors can just take a deep breath and listen to what's being said in a rational way after Liberation Day, I think I was on this network, many other networks. And I said, why doesn't everyone just take a deep breath? The tariffs you were seeing are the highest tariffs. You're going to see if there's no retaliation. And the only country that retaliated was China. The market sold off. I can't remember about 14, 13, 14 percent. And then we had the fastest recovery ever. So anyone who sold then just wasn't listening. And it was the same, it was kind of the same thing. You know, I will point out that since the, I announced the increased buyback size that we've had a surge in oil prices, global rates are up around the world. How much is the 30-year treasury up?
96:BESSENT: Yeah, I'm not going to talk about whether I agree with it or not. But the, I have great confidence in Chair Warsh. More importantly, the president has great confidence in him, and we are sure that he will do the right thing to balance the inflation mandate versus the growth mandate. And we'll see that, we will see whether this is the, a supply shock on the energy side, but thus far, core inflation has been a very quiescent. And we, so we haven't seen an uptick in that. Everything is in the headline inflation.
97:KERNEN: All right. Well, you let us know next time you're in town because it's much better when you're on set. And I will have those waffles and chicken waiting.

On September 10, 2026, Anthropic published its most detailed threat intelligence report to date, covering nine months of documented misuse of its Claude AI models from December 2025 through August 2026.

## The Five Cases

The new report outlines five real-life case studies in which users "circumvented controls" that block users from specific regions and "engaged in other efforts to obfuscate the purpose of their research to evade our safeguards." The examples include possible gain-of-function research and involve both infectious diseases, such as bird flu, and novel venoms and toxins.

Specific cases detailed include:

- One of the case studies detailed in the report involved a request for assistance writing a grant application for funding of gain-of-function research on the transmissibility and immune evasion of the chikungunya virus.

- In another case, a researcher outside the US was using Claude for work on bird flu that focused on viruses' adaptation to mammals and how it caused severe illness.

- The report also details cases on research into orthopoxviruses – a group that includes variola, which causes smallpox, and mpox – as well as venom toxins.

## Broader Context

The AI company known for its Claude model said it considers biological misuse one of the "most serious risks" to artificial intelligence models. Looking over 30 days of activity, Anthropic said, it identified about 35 "distinct research efforts" with potentially concerning activity.

Key Points

- Chinese AI models have rapidly gained traction in 2026, with their token usage surging on developer platforms OpenRouter and Vercel.

- Lower prices and strong performance are helping drive adoption, particularly for coding and other agentic tasks, although U.S. frontier models still attract more overall spending.

- The shift is drawing scrutiny in Washington, where lawmakers are investigating the growing use of Chinese AI amid concerns about technology competition, security and Beijing’s global influence.

AI was a major focus as U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping met this week.
The most advanced U.S. models lead most benchmarks, but Chinese companies like DeepSeek, Z.ai and Alibaba have released new models with major performance gains in tasks such as coding.

According to usage data shared with CNBC, the global adoption of Chinese models by companies has increased substantially in 2026.
Chinese AI models have gone from a relatively small share of usage to a majority on two major developer platforms that provide gateways for companies to access models from different providers. On OpenRouter, they accounted for 57%-67% of tokens used in the week of Sept. 14, up from 6%-13% in February. On Vercel, their share rose to 55% in August from 11% in January.

OpenRouter's data related to companies in the U.S., Europe and what it defines as the "Global South" — 82 countries across Central and South America, Africa, and Asia. Vercel did not specify its data's geographical breakdown.
Concern is growing in Washington, where two U.S. House Committees are investigating the impact of rising adoption of Chinese models.
The U.S. has sought to preserve its AI lead by restricting Chinese AI companies from buying the most advanced chips through export controls.

Washington is concerned about them accessing Nvidia chips remotely , via overseas data centers, and gaining ground by using "distillation" where new models mimic older, more established ones.

Chinese AI represents "real economic and security risks for the United States," said Daniel Remler, a senior fellow in the technology and national security program at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS), a think tank.
"The ultimate concern is that the integration of Chinese AI models pulls countries into a Chinese technology sphere of influence that hardens into geopolitical alignment," he told CNBC.
Peter Walker, head of insights at OpenRouter, told CNBC, Chinese open source models released this year "can credibly perform in advanced agentic use cases, especially in regards to coding, in a way that was just not true in late 2025."
They're also "incredibly cost-effective compared to most models from American labs," he added.
Earlier this week, OpenAI and Anthropic both announced new, cheaper models. Dianne Penn, head of product management, research and labs at Anthropic, told CNBC that the company was trying to make its models answers "more efficient, so it uses less tokens depending on your effort setting."

Price is key in rising adoption of Chinese models, Harpreet Arora, head of agentic infrastructure at Vercel, told CNBC. "Chinese models are becoming capable enough for more tasks at a much lower cost. Once a model meets the quality bar for the job, that price difference becomes compelling."
But he added that companies still want to use frontier U.S. models for some more complicated tasks.

Businesses in what OpenRouter defines as "Global South" have been the biggest users of Chinese AI models on the company's system in recent weeks.
More than two-thirds — 67% — of the tokens these companies use are on Chinese models. About half the tokens on OpenRouter are used by companies in the U.S.
"Southeast Asia in particular may see significant uptake of Chinese AI models given the close economic and cultural linkages [with China] plus growing digital infrastructure," said CNAS' Remler.

Sep. 28, 2026

China has quietly escalated one of its most consequential tech-sector policies. The government has extended overseas travel restrictions to include the family members of leading AI and chip executives at private companies, requiring government pre-approval before relatives can leave the country.

The move, reported by Bloomberg on September 28, 2026, marks a sharp widening of measures that first appeared in May 2026, when Beijing began mandating travel pre-approval for top AI professionals at firms including Alibaba and DeepSeek .

Advertisement

# How the restrictions evolved

DeepSeek employees began surrendering passports around March 2026, a timeline that coincides with the public release of the company’s R1 model. That same month, authorities imposed exit bans on the co-founders of Manus AI amid scrutiny of a major acquisition the startup was pursuing.

By May 2026, the restrictions had formalized into a pre-approval requirement covering top professionals at private-sector AI firms broadly. September 15, 2026 brought another turn: nationwide rules took effect that formalize penalties specifically tied to violations of industrial and technological security, giving the exit-ban framework a firmer legal backbone.

We respect your privacy. Unsubscribe anytime.

Now, two weeks after those rules went live, the net has widened again. Family members of key executives are now subject to the same pre-approval requirement, meaning a spouse or child booking an international trip is effectively asking the government for permission.

# What Beijing is trying to protect

The shift from state-linked individuals to private-sector talent is significant on its own. For years, exit bans and travel controls were associated primarily with government officials, state enterprise executives, and people under direct legal scrutiny. Applying the same tools to engineers and researchers at startups is a different category of intervention entirely.

# British Columbia sued OpenAI over ChatGPT's role in a deadly Canadian school shooting
The province filed suit in California federal court, alleging OpenAI failed to warn police after flagging the shooter's ChatGPT activity

By Cris Tolomia · 2 min read · Updated September 22, 2026

Add QZ to Google

SeongJoon Cho / Bloomberg via Getty Images

British Columbia filed a lawsuit against OpenAI and its chief executive, Sam Altman, on Monday in U.S. District Court in Northern California, alleging the company's failure to notify law enforcement of threats made through ChatGPT contributed to a mass shooting at a Tumbler Ridge secondary school that killed nine people.

The February 10 attack killed an educational assistant and five students aged 12 to 13 at Tumbler Ridge Secondary school, as well as the shooter's mother and stepbrother, according to Reuters . The shooter, 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar, died by suicide at the scene. The town of roughly 2,700 people saw one of the worst mass killings in Canada in years, according to the Wall Street Journal .

Van Rootselaar's ChatGPT account came to OpenAI's attention in June 2025, when her conversations revealed repeated references to gun violence across multiple days. Members of OpenAI's safety team pushed to alert law enforcement, but were overruled by Altman and other senior leaders, according to the Wall Street Journal, which obtained accounts from OpenAI whistleblowers after the massacre. After her original account was shut down, Van Rootselaar opened a new one and kept using the service to plot the attack, according to Reuters.

Among its claims, the 39-page complaint charges that OpenAI put a dangerous product into the market, fell short of product liability requirements, and bore responsibility for facilitating a mass shooting, according to the Wall Street Journal. The province is seeking damages to cover costs it has incurred and will incur in recovering from the attack, including mental health care and a replacement school — the building where the shooting occurred is being demolished — as well as a court order directing changes to how OpenAI handles ChatGPT conversations that could lead to violence, according to Reuters.

"In any other circumstance where a person aids, encourages or conspires to commit a criminal offense or is criminally negligent, they can be investigated, prosecuted and judged," British Columbia Attorney General Niki Sharma said in a statement. "There is no AI exemption to those criminal law principles."

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri called the Tumbler Ridge shooting an unspeakable tragedy and said the company remains committed to working with government and law enforcement officials, according to Reuters.

British Columbia's suit follows lawsuits filed by more than 30 family members of victims in California federal court. In June, Florida became the first U.S. state to sue OpenAI over safety risks, accusing the company of misrepresenting the safety of ChatGPT.

OpenAI has declined to release Van Rootselaar's ChatGPT logs to the province, Sharma said, though the company said it has provided the logs to law enforcement and has offered to cooperate with plaintiffs on discovery, according to the Wall Street Journal.

At the UN and in Washington, Leaders Clash on Approach to AI | TechPolicy.Press Newsletter

# At the UN and in Washington, Leaders Clash on Approach to AI
Justin Hendrix / Sep 27, 2026 The Tech Policy Press newsletter is published every Sunday. Subscribe here to receive it in your email inbox .
CEO of OpenAI Sam Altman speaks during a United Nations Security Council meeting on artificial intelligence and international security under “Maintenance of International Peace and Security” on September 23, 2026 in New York City. Tech industry leaders including the CEOs of OpenAI, Anthropic and Hugging Face briefed ambassadors on the risks of artificial intelligence. (Photo by Alexi J. Rosenfeld/Getty Images)

Republish

Share

Good morning!
It was great to see so many from across the Tech Policy Press community in New York this week. Folks traveled in for the United Nations General Assembly, Climate Week and related events. Artificial intelligence and the concentration of tech power was a topic of discussion in the General Assembly hall and at debates and discussions hosted in smaller venues across the city.

- In his speech, UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned that “we are witnessing an extraordinary transfer of power away from governments to a handful of private corporations and individuals,” and cautioned that “technological power alone cannot guarantee security.” He said humanity must govern artificial intelligence “before it governs us.”

- AI executives and experts gave speeches in the Security Council, including OpenAI’s Sam Altman , Anthropic’s Dario Amodei , Hugging Face’s Clément Delangue , and Yoshua Bengio , co-chair of the UN’s scientific panel on AI. Altman warned that “we could lose control of the future to AI. The risk is that it moves so fast that people can no longer follow what's happening or intervene when needed.”

- The United States underscored its bid for AI dominance. President Donald Trump , in his speech before the General Assembly, rejected “any attempt to construct a globalist scheme of control for the Artificial Intelligence being spoken of so much now — hereinafter officially called ‘Super Intelligence.’” White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) director Michael Kratsios also pushed the terminology change, referencing American leadership in “superintelligence, formerly known as AI” in his speech.

- China’s ambassador, Fu Cong , took a different tact , emphasizing the various ways that China aims to promote international collaboration and invest in AI development in other regions of the world. He said the “international community should strengthen solidarity and cooperation, attach equal importance to development and security, and promote AI globally for the positive, for good and for humanity, thereby contributing to world peace, stability, development and prosperity.”

- France’s President Emmanuel Macron called for a "coalition of the independents" to pool compute resources and build a shared open-source frontier model, and for states to refuse to become "vassals" of either superpower.

- In his first appearance at the UN as UK prime minister, Andy Burnham announced a US-UK AI defense partnership and said he will put AI at the heart of the UK's G20 presidency.

- European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen spoke at the high-level dialogue on protecting children's rights facing AI. “Our children are engaging with some of the most sophisticated technology ever created. And it was not created with children's wellbeing or development in mind,” she said.

- Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez , called for strict regulation on "tecno-oligarcas," while Bangladesh prime minister Tarique Rahman said , “We do not want today's digital divide to become tomorrow's artificial intelligence divide.”

- Some expressed concern about over-regulation. Nigeria’s vice president, Kashim Shettima , said “We refuse to surrender our technological future to paranoia.” Argentina President Javier Milei said state control over AI means granting the government “the power to limit what others may create.”
We had multiple pieces that addressed concerns around the UN, AI and human rights on Tech Policy Press this week.

- Chris Stokel-Walker reported on whether the UN can turn talk into action as frontier labs call for a slowdown.

- Amid warnings of runaway AI systems and even human extinction, Jenny Domino , an S.J.D. candidate at Harvard Law School, and Jen Weedon , researcher and lecturer at Columbia University’s School of International Affairs’ Institute for Global Politics, say an important question remains : "what is AI doing to people, communities, and their rights, right now?"

- Claiming without evidence that AI will be a "great equalizer" is yet another example of global powers and tech oligarchs distorting reality and disregarding African lives, argues Alison Gillwald , an adjunct professor at the University of Cape Town’s Nelson Mandela School of Public Governance and founding director of Research ICT Africa.

- Jane Munga of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace writes that even as the UN focuses on AI governance issues, including "rogue" agents and risks, it also needs to prioritize the resilience of the undersea cables that carry the data that enables communications and AI applications.

# US-China AI dialogue
The other big news this week on the international stage was the Trump-Xi summit in Washington, D.C. The two leaders agreed to ongoing dialogue on AI issues and a communications channel to discuss serious AI security incidents. We had a handful of pieces that addressed questions related to the US-China AI dialogue.

- "Worms" are a type of malware that can self-replicate and autonomously spread across networks. Howard Fei , a master’s candidate at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Study, argues Trump and Xi have a narrow window to agree on limits for AI-enabled adaptive worms before a shared risk becomes a shared crisis.

- Trump says data center opposition is a Chinese psy-op. Chinese state media says US AI safety calls are a psy-op. Oxford China Policy Lab's Elisabeth Siegel says both accusations point to the same problem: no one can independently verify what AI companies claim .

- The US should make it a national priority to develop safer open-weight models , says AI policy researcher and lawyer Simon Hedlin — or cede the global ecosystem to China. “If both countries are developing frontier open-weight models, there is a symmetry that makes it easier to agree to mutual safety standards because the two governments’ commitments will be comparable,” he writes.

# The US surveillance state

- Sarah Engelberg-Nolan , Emma Haberman and Nicole Brosnan, J.D. candidates at Fordham University School of Law, carefully map out the legal questions raised by ICE's use of Palantir's Enhanced Leads Identification & Targeting for Enforcement (ELITE) targeting tool, from Fourth Amendment search issues to due process and standing hurdles. This is a must-read this week.

- Relatedly, Democracy Forward research analyst Emily Froude argues that DHS is exploiting a loophole in the Trump administration's own AI policy — the "principal basis" standard — to avoid classifying its immigration enforcement AI tools as high-impact and evade disclosure requirements.

- From lantern laws to Black Codes to COINTELPRO to today: facial recognition turns the border into "a network of surveillance that digitizes colonial logic and sorts bodies into categories of belonging and threat along racial lines," argue Tsion Gurmu , Nekessa Opoti and Fatima Mohamed of the Black Alliance for Just Immigration (BAJI).

- Flock is "a visible manifestation of a much larger transformation in American surveillance that should alarm Americans." As a Senate Judiciary subcommittee examines Flock's surveillance network , Michael De Dora (Access Now) and Maria Villegas Bravo (EPIC) laid out the case against the company's cameras and what policymakers can do about them just ahead of last week’s Senate subcommittee hearing on the subject.

# Our content delivered to your inbox.
Join our newsletter on issues and ideas at the intersection of tech & democracy

# Thank you!
You have successfully joined our subscriber list.

# The EU rulebook in practice

- The European Union says its AI rules already give regulators the tools to deal with the risks posed by increasingly capable AI models . Legal experts are questioning how far those powers actually extend. “Since August, the AI Office's new powers allow the European regulators to ask providers to restrict a model’s availability on the EU market, withdraw it or recall it. But experts disagree over how those powers can be used in the kinds of testing incidents now making headlines,” journalist Joana Soares reports.

- The EU's out-of-court dispute system was designed to improve content moderation accuracy. David Sullivan , Jonny Shipp and Farzaneh Badiei of the Digital Trust and Safety Partnership argue the fee structure intended to increase quality has been replaced with one that drives quantity.

- A new report by the Atlantic Council’s Democracy + Tech Initiative and Global Disinformation Index finds that Europe's Democracy Stack relies heavily on US government and philanthropic funding. Tech Policy Press contributing editor Mark Scott and Global Disinformation Index policy research director Richard Woods on what the findings reveal and what Brussels needs to do about it.

- The choice for Europe is not between regulating and building. It is between continuing to set rules for infrastructure that others operate, and acquiring the capacity to operate infrastructure whose rules Europe sets and can change , writes Nicholas Gates , senior policy advisor at OpenForum Europe.

# Safer social media for children

- Unlike Australia's ban, John Matheson, senior tech policy fellow at McGill University's Centre for Media, Technology, and Democracy, and Canada Director at Reset Tech, writes, Canada's Safe Social Media Act asks a different question: not whether to keep children off social media, but whether platforms can be built to deserve them. “Democracies are converging on age limits and stronger platform regulation because parents are demanding action. A simple ban, however, protects children from social media without ever making social media fit for them,” he writes.

- The EU Kids Act would allow guardians to use interoperable third-party tools on Very Large Online Platforms. Independent tech policy analyst Aahil Sheikh writes that this approach could restore control to users when platform-based safety measures fail.

- The EU Kids Act adds a new layer to an already dense regulatory landscape . Jessica Galissaire , senior policy researcher in the Interface’s Strengthening the Digital Public Sphere and Platform Regulation program, unpacks how it relates to the Digital Services Act, AI Act and Digital Fairness Act, and what that means for the EU's online safety enforcement.

- Maddie Freeman , a survivor of social media addiction and mental health crises and a Public Voices Fellow on Youth Well-Being and Power with The OpEd Project and Hopelab, created a youth-led movement to help teens detox from tech . She says Meta’s recent settlement deal does not address the root causes of the harms she experienced.

# AI, digital public infrastructure & sovereignty

- A long list of countries are exploring the development of biometric identity and payment transfer systems based on India's digital public infrastructure . Lawyers Mustafa Rajkotwala and Dhruv Jadhav say it's high time for key legal rights to be defined.

- All five of the main presidential hopefuls in Brazil's upcoming election feature "sovereignty" prominently in their plans. But it means entirely different things to each candidate, from right to left, reports Tech Policy Press fellow Tatiana Dias .

# Abstract
The absence of accurate, noninvasive, scalable screening tools keeps early esophageal cancer (EC) detection a global health challenge. Although noncontrast computed tomography (NC CT) is widely accessible, the esophagus is a hollow tubular structure prone to collapse and motion artifacts, making small early malignant lesions difficult to distinguish from normal tissue. Here we developed the Esophageal AI-Guided malignant Lesion Evaluation (EAGLE) model to detect precancerous lesions and cancer from chest NC CT, a task historically considered impossible. EAGLE was trained on 6,813 patients from two centers and validated across 12 centers in three countries involving 80,612 patients in opportunistic and population-based screening settings. For opportunistic screening on existing CT scans, multicenter external test cohorts (eight centers, n  = 11,466) achieved 98.5% specificity, with 90.0% sensitivity for cancer and 52.5% for precancerous lesions; low-dose CT (LDCT) validation (two centers, n  = 1,607) showed comparable performance, supporting EC screening through lung-cancer screening programs. Calibration in a real-world cohort (three centers, n  = 35,402) reduced false positives by 72.7% while preserving sensitivity; prospective hospital validation ( n  = 17,446) achieved a 42.2% PPV, and real-world low-dose screening ( n  = 10,959) reached 99.94% specificity. EAGLE also detected precancerous lesions—in paired CT–endoscopy cohorts (two centers, n  = 702), sensitivities were 65.0% for precancerous lesions and 78.4% for stage I EC at a higher-sensitivity operating point. Exploratory analyses of a prospectively enrolled cohort suggest that referring high-risk individuals for endoscopy could improve screening efficiency. In conclusion, EAGLE has the potential to serve as a scalable tool for early EC screening. Chictr.org.cn identifier: ChiCTR2300074806 .

# Main
Esophageal cancer (EC) is one of the most common digestive tract cancers worldwide, with estimated 511,000 new cases and 445,000 deaths in 2022 (ref. 1 ). EC comprises two major histological subtypes, esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC), which differ substantially in their risk factors, anatomical locations and geographic distributions. It remains a critical global health issue, characterized by high mortality rates due to its frequent diagnosis at advanced stages and the absence of formalized screening programs 2 , 3 . Although the prognosis of EC has improved in the past decades, survival remains unsatisfactory, as the 5-year overall survival rates are 36.9% in China and 18.5% in the United States 4 , 5 . While high-risk population-based endoscopic screening has made a substantial contribution to the early detection and intervention of EC in China 6 , 7 , 8 , its invasive nature and low compliance make it impractical for large-scale screening of asymptomatic populations globally, particularly in countries and regions lacking adequate endoscopy infrastructure. Nonendoscopic methods, such as liquid biopsy 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 and sponge cytology 14 , 15 , have been evaluated for EC screening, but the moderate sensitivity in early-stage cancer, the substantial costs and the requirement of several visits to the clinics pose challenges for their wide implementation. An accurate, noninvasive, cost-effective and rapid tool for worldwide EC screening remains an unsolved clinical problem.
Noncontrast computed tomography (NC CT) is a widely used medical imaging protocol in routine clinical visits and physical examinations, showing characteristics that are noninvasive, cost-effective and rapid 16 . However, identifying esophageal malignancies on NC CT is challenging even for experienced radiologists, largely because early-stage esophageal malignant lesions can be extremely small, often confined to the epithelial layer (high-grade intraepithelial neoplasia, HGIN) or invading only the mucosa or submucosa (stage I). In addition, the esophagus is a thoracic organ with a long, narrow tubular structure and is therefore frequently affected by physiological collapse and susceptible to motion from the heart and great vessels, making subtle lesions difficult to distinguish from normal tissue and limiting the utility of CT for EC screening. Consistent with this, a recent study revealed that the majority of individuals who died from EC had no suspicious esophageal findings documented in their chest NC CT reports within the preceding 5 years 17 . Recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have shown that data-driven models can detect subtle lesions on medical images 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , and have highlighted the potential of AI approaches to improve cancer screening 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 , offering an avenue for early EC detection on NC CT. Enabling EC screening could open new possibilities for chest NC CT scans (40% of all CT examinations 28 ) that already cover the full esophagus, including both regular-dose CT obtained during clinical visits and LDCT used in lung-cancer screening programs. Particularly, given that LDCT lung-cancer screening is now performed worldwide, and smoking is a shared risk factor for lung and ECs 29 , 30 , integrating EC detection into LDCT workflows may enable a one-scan, multicancer screening paradigm without requiring additional imaging procedures. At the same time, LDCT introduces an additional level of difficulty for esophageal lesion detection because it has lower image quality and increased noise.
In this study, we present Esophageal AI-Guided malignant Lesion Evaluation (EAGLE; Fig. 1 ), a new AI model that not only identifies EC but also detects malignant precancerous lesions (HGIN). This capability supports the potential expansion of AI from opportunistic finding to active population-based prevention—it not only achieves high accuracy in opportunistically identifying malignancies missed by the standard of care (SOC), but also improves efficiency in population-based endoscopic screening. For ‘opportunistic screening’, where EAGLE operates at high specificity, multicenter reader studies showed that it significantly enhances radiologists’ ability to identify early cancers while lowering the false-positive (FP) rate; large-scale multicenter external validation across three countries confirmed its generalizability in hospital scenarios; a simulation training strategy demonstrated comparable specificity and sensitivity to those achieved with regular-dose scans in an LDCT cohort; and large-scale real-world studies recalibrated the model to markedly lower the FP rate without sacrificing sensitivity, confirmed exceptionally high specificity in a consecutive physical examination LDCT cohort and demonstrated a clinically desirable positive predictive value (PPV) in a prospective hospital validation.
Fig. 1: Overview of the EAGLE development, validation and clinical integration framework.
Full size image

a , AI model development. EAGLE was designed to process NC CT scans for EC diagnosis, output binary classification (positive/negative), malignant lesion masks and heatmaps that highlight regions contributing to diagnostic decisions. EAGLE was trained on CT datasets from two medical centers, and each malignant case included histopathology-confirmed labels and expert-annotated lesion masks. b , Multiscenario evaluation. Validation of opportunistic screening in the hospital, including an internal validation cohort, an external validation cohort across eight centers from three countries (China, Czech Republic and Australia), a reader study, a large-scale real-world study and a prospective validation. Validation in existing LDCT-based programs, including a retrospective assessment on two centers, and a real-world LDCT cohort. c , AI-guided optimization of existing clinical workflows. Four strategic implementation scenarios demonstrate EAGLE’s potential to enhance existing EC care pathways. CAM, class activation mapping; w/o, without.

EAGLE also showed potential to boost established ‘population-based endoscopic screening programs’, where it operates at a high sensitivity threshold to minimize the risk of missed cancers—we retrospectively evaluated performance on NC CT scans from individuals who underwent endoscopic screening at two external centers, and integrated EAGLE into a standard endoscopic screening workflow for a prospectively enrolled high-risk cohort, where simulation analysis suggested that using EAGLE for pre-endoscopy risk stratification could markedly reduce unnecessary endoscopic procedures while preserving cancer detection, thereby improving the detection rate and coverage of current endoscopic screening programs.

# Results

# The EAGLE model
EAGLE identifies high-risk patients with malignant esophageal lesions using NC CT scans, outputting binary classification (positive or negative), malignant lesion segmentation masks and classification heatmaps that highlight regions contributing to diagnostic decisions (Fig. 1a ). Positive cases were defined as malignant esophageal lesions, including histology-confirmed esophageal carcinoma (EC) and HGIN. Negative controls were patients without EC and HGIN, who were confirmed by at least 2 years of clinical follow-up or negative endoscopic screening within 1 year in the retrospective datasets. The standard of truth for all cohorts is provided in Supplementary Table 3 . EAGLE was trained on a two-center cohort of NC CT scans from 6,813 patients (264 = HGIN, 548 = stage I, 2,932 = stages II–IV and 3,069 = negative controls) from Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center (SYSUCC) and Sichuan Cancer Hospital (SCCH). The patient characteristics are shown in Extended Data Table 1 . Besides patient-level classification labels, EAGLE was also supervised by voxel-wise annotations, including both the esophagus and malignant lesions. We recruited an annotation team to perform a rigorous annotation procedure using the cloud-based DAMO MED annotation system (Extended Data Fig. 1 and Methods ).
EAGLE is a two-stage approach—the first stage localizes the esophagus within the entire three-dimensional (3D) CT scan and the second stage simultaneously segments lesions and predicts the esophageal malignant probability for the patient.
