The Labs Are Building Their Own Safety Body. Three Days After the Second Training Halt, That Is the Story. – Forkast

Skip to content
Skip to content

In the wake of OpenAI’s second training halt and explicit liability signals from the Treasury Secretary, the industry’s largest players have moved to formalize a self-regulatory body: the Standards Authority for Frontier AI. Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic are proposing a structure modeled after the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority – common safety benchmarks, standardized model testing, voluntary safety commitments, auditor qualifications, and incident reporting protocols. The target launch is late 2026 or early 2027. The concept, first attributed to Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis in July 2026, has been under active discussion for weeks.

The timing is not coincidental. SAFA arrives in the same window as OpenAI’s second training halt , Treasury Secretary Bessent’s explicit rejection of liability shields, and an antitrust lawsuit that alleges safety coordination is cartel behavior. The labs are building the gate while the legal system is testing whether the gate itself is the problem.

# What SAFA Would Do

The proposed body would establish common testing and risk-assessment practices for frontier models, support third-party testing organizations, set standards for independent auditors, and potentially conduct some model evaluations itself. Several figures have been approached for leadership roles, including former White House AI policy adviser Sriram Krishnan, former Biden administration technology official Arati Prabhakar, former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, and venture capitalist David Friedberg.

The scope is broad. But the enforcement question remains open. If SAFA operates on voluntary commitments – which all reporting to date suggests – it creates a structure where compliance is a signal, not a constraint. Labs that choose not to participate face no formal consequence. Labs that do participate gain the credibility of third-party oversight without the accountability that comes with mandatory compliance.

# Lehane’s Lobbying and the Policy Window

OpenAI’s Chief Global Affairs Officer, Chris Lehane, confirmed the discussions on September 15 to Bloomberg, CNBC, and TechCrunch. Lehane has been in Washington meeting with lawmakers on catastrophic AI risks. On September 9, he published an OpenAI blog post titled “The AI policy window is open. We need to act.” – a three-pillar framework calling for mandatory national safety requirements, state-level momentum, and industry-led standards.

Advertisement

Lehane also publicly supports a provision in the FRONTIER Act that would require frontier labs to allow “independent verification organizations” into their companies. This positioning is careful: OpenAI is calling for third-party oversight while simultaneously defining the terms of that oversight. The company published its own third-party assessment framework on September 22 – unilaterally setting the methodology for the scrutiny it faces.

# Who Is Not at the Table

The industry is far from unified. At Dreamforce on September 15, Meta, xAI, and Nvidia publicly opposed the formation of SAFA. Mark Zuckerberg argued that AI labs already face strong liability incentives and that existing laws are sufficient. Jensen Huang of Nvidia went further, telling Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff that AI laws are “just completely unnecessary” and that model makers should simply take responsibility for their products. xAI opposed alongside both companies.

The opposition is not marginal. Meta and xAI are building frontier models. Nvidia supplies the compute infrastructure. Their refusal to join SAFA means the body would launch without the participation of at least two frontier-capable model builders and the dominant hardware supplier. A safety standards body that excludes its most aggressive competitors is not a safety body – it is a competitive positioning play with safety branding.

# The Antitrust Shadow

SAFA arrives in a hostile legal and political environment. On September 15, Senators Hawley and Cruz blocked an antitrust exemption in the NDAA that would have provided legal cover for coordinated safety standards. Three days later, four plaintiffs filed Buist et al. v. Anthropic PBC et al. , alleging that safety coordination among competitors constitutes an output-restricting cartel under Section 1 of the Sherman Act. Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez has labeled the proposed body “a cartel by any other name.”

On September 19, President Trump dismissed AI safety as a “hoax” and announced the creation of an AI Force with no safety mandate. The White House has put a draft executive order on hold, telling the companies to reach industry consensus first. The political environment does not merely fail to support self-regulation – it actively questions whether self-regulation is distinguishable from market manipulation.

# The Structural Question

The core tension of SAFA is governance. When the largest players in an industry define the safety benchmarks, the risk of regulatory capture is inherent. If SAFA becomes the de facto standard-setter, it creates a compliance barrier for smaller startups that cannot afford the costs of meeting those benchmarks – benchmarks defined by the incumbents who can.

The FINRA comparison is instructive. FINRA succeeded because Congress granted it statutory authority through the Securities Exchange Act. Without equivalent legislative backing, SAFA operates as a voluntary pact among competitors – which is precisely what the antitrust lawsuit alleges is illegal. The body can launch. But without legislative authority, every standard it sets is simultaneously a safety claim and a potential exhibit in the next cartel filing.

The labs that proposed SAFA are the same ones being sued for coordinating on safety. They are building the oversight mechanism while the legal system tests whether the oversight mechanism is the crime. The outcome of that test will determine whether SAFA becomes a governance milestone or a structural footnote in the era when safety coordination was legally possible.

Chris Lehane’s OpenAI blog post is confirmed by search but returned HTTP 403 from Cloudflare. Dreamforce opposition confirmed via CNBC. Candidate leadership names confirmed via multiple secondary sources. BankInfoSecurity, CIO.com, Yahoo News, YourStory, ROIC.ai, and TheStreet corroborate the core details.

## Recent Policy and Research

In July 2026, the White House released the United States Government Policy for Stopping High-Risk Life Sciences Research (2026 policy), pursuant to Executive Order 14292, "Improving the Safety and Security of Biological Research." This executive order directed OSTP to revise or replace the 2024 Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening, which required recipients of federal funding for this research to purchase services only from companies that followed certain synthesis screening procedures. However, OSTP has not updated the 2024 framework to date.

## AI and Biosecurity Challenges

Sequence-based screening measures are no longer sufficient as standalone safeguards in a landscape shaped by AI-assisted biological design, as protein language models and generative design tools may expand the sequence design space in ways that are harder to assess through homology-based screening alone.

Research identified a vulnerability where AI-redesigned sequences could not be detected reliably by current tools used by nucleic acid synthesis providers.

## Governance Proposals

The Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act of 2026 would require binding regulations including sequence screening, customer verification, split-order detection across providers, a regularly updated list of sequences of concern, provider auditing and conformity assessment, and civil enforcement for violations. However, the bill stalled in committee, leaving much of the private DNA synthesis market outside of binding federal oversight.

# Fact-verification report — AI in clinical/scientific practice, 21–27 Sep 2026

All 11 URLs were taken from the repo's own daily JSON files. All 11 opened. No archive/cache mirrors used. Two Nature URLs refused WebFetch (303 to idp.nature.com) and were retrieved with `node scripts/fetch.js`.

---

## 1. Nature Medicine — esophageal cancer CT model
**URL:** https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-026-04656-4
**OPENS:** yes (via `scripts/fetch.js`; WebFetch 303-redirects to idp.nature.com). Full text available.
**PUBLISHED:** Received 22 July 2026 · Accepted 17 August 2026 · **Published: 22 September 2026** (no time/timezone shown)
**Title:** "Large-scale esophageal cancer screening through noncontrast computed tomography and artificial intelligence"

**CONFIRMED**
1. Model name: "Esophageal AI-Guided malignant Lesion Evaluation (EAGLE)".
2. "EAGLE was trained on 6,813 patients from two centers and validated across 12 centers in three countries involving 80,612 patients in opportunistic and population-based screening settings."
3. Training cohort breakdown: "6,813 patients (264 = HGIN, 548 = stage I, 2,932 = stages II–IV and 3,069 = negative controls)" from Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center (SYSUCC) and Sichuan Cancer Hospital (SCCH).
4. "multicenter external test cohorts (eight centers, n = 11,466) achieved 98.5% specificity, with 90.0% sensitivity for cancer and 52.5% for precancerous lesions".
5. "low-dose CT (LDCT) validation (two centers, n = 1,607) showed comparable performance".
6. "Calibration in a real-world cohort (three centers, n = 35,402) reduced false positives by 72.7% while preserving sensitivity".
7. "prospective hospital validation (n = 17,446) achieved a 42.2% PPV".
8. "real-world low-dose screening (n = 10,959) reached 99.94% specificity".
9. "in paired CT–endoscopy cohorts (two centers, n = 702), sensitivities were 65.0% for precancerous lesions and 78.4% for stage I EC at a higher-sensitivity operating point."
10. Three countries named: China, Czech Republic and Australia.
11. Trial registration: "Chictr.org.cn identifier: ChiCTR2300074806".
12. Context figures cited: "511,000 new cases and 445,000 deaths in 2022"; 5-year overall survival "36.9% in China and 18.5% in the United States"; chest NC CT is "40% of all CT examinations".
13. Two-stage architecture; negative controls "confirmed by at least 2 years of clinical follow-up or negative endoscopic screening within 1 year in the retrospective datasets."

**NOT SAID**
- No claim of mortality reduction, survival benefit or stage-shift benefit. The 98.5% specificity figure is from a **retrospective multicentre external test set (n=11,466)**, not from the full 80,612 and not from the prospective arm.
- The endoscopy-referral efficiency finding is hedged: "Exploratory analyses of a prospectively enrolled cohort **suggest** that referring high-risk individuals for endoscopy **could** improve screening efficiency," and the conclusion is only "EAGLE **has the potential to** serve as a scalable tool for early EC screening."
- No randomised comparison against standard of care; no cost-effectiveness result; no claim of regulatory clearance.

---

## 2. medRxiv — multi-modal model, 195 diseases, UK Biobank
**URL:** https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.09.19.26363460v1
**OPENS:** yes
**PUBLISHED:** "Posted September 21, 2026." (v1) — DOI stamp 2026.09.19
**Title:** "A world model simulates the latent dynamics of human health" (model: **HealthFlux**)
**Authors include:** Zirui Wang, Odin Zhang, … James Zou, Michael P. Snyder, Vadim N. Gladyshev, Tony Wyss-Coray, Kejun Ying

**CONFIRMED** (verbatim from abstract)
1. "learns the latent dynamics of health from 5,647 features across eleven data domains, spanning clinical records, blood tests, genetics, proteomics, metabolomics and MRI, in 502,166 UK Biobank participants."
2. "In held-out participants, HealthFlux predicts 195 diseases and death over five years with a mean AUROC of 0.816, compared with 0.715 for the previous state-of-the-art model."
3. "These results remain true when validated in three independent cohorts, and HealthFlux also outperforms specialized clinical risk scores for disease and mortality."
4. "Simulated forward without further observations, the state continues to predict disease accurately up to a decade after the last measurement."
5. "HealthFlux predicts diseases excluded entirely from training, with a mean AUROC of 0.769".
6. Architecture: "hybrid state-space architecture combines ODE-based evolution between observations with continuous-time recurrent updates when new measurements arrive."

**NOT SAID**
- Not peer reviewed. No clinical deployment, no prospective validation, no clinician-in-the-loop test, no claim of improved patient outcomes, no causal mechanism claim. The 0.816 is a held-out **retrospective** cohort metric, not a real-workflow result. The generalisation claim ("evidence that it has learned health itself rather than the diseases it was trained on") is the authors' inference from AUROC 0.769 on held-out disease labels, not a demonstrated clinical property.

---

## 3. npj Digital Medicine — junior clinicians and GPT-4o hallucinations
**URL:** https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03294-x
**OPENS:** yes (via `scripts/fetch.js`; WebFetch 303-redirects). **Abstract + metadata only** — the served HTML does not include the Results/Methods body, so cohort counts below the abstract level are not on the page as retrieved.
**PUBLISHED:** Received 07 May 2026 · Accepted 13 September 2026 · **Published: 24 September 2026**
**Title:** "A multicenter assessment of human oversight of generative AI outputs in simulated clinical decision making"
**Authors/institutions:** Yunyun Zhang & Jiacheng Zhou (equal contribution), Zhiyong Zhang, Jintao Zhang, Rongrong Wan, Hua Guo, Xiaochuan Cui, Bingbing Fu, Jia Meng, Bo Yue — Affiliated Wuxi People's Hospital of Nanjing Medical University; First Affiliated Hospital of Jiamusi University; Second Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University; Second Affiliated Hospital of Qiqihar Medical University (all China).

**CONFIRMED** (verbatim)
1. "In this multi-center cross-sectional study, we systematically detected and classified GPT-4o-generated hallucinations across diverse clinical scenarios."
2. "Our results revealed that only 15.8% of hallucinations were identified, and 13.1% of clinicians failed to detect any hallucinations across all scenarios."
3. "Notably, detection rates did not improve with increasing clinical risk, and variability in hallucination detection arose primarily from between-clinician rather than between-scenario differences."
4. "Our findings reveal a critical gap between technical validation and real-world clinical use."
5. "These results indicate that future clinical applications will require well-designed, structured human-AI collaborative workflows, along with tiered clinical certification pathways, to ensure patient safety."
6. "Current safeguards rely on a 'clinician-in-the-loop' model, which assumes that clinicians can reliably identify and correct these hallucinations."
7. LLM disclosure: "GPT-4o (OpenAI) was accessed via the web-based ChatGPT interface in **July 2024**"; "training data having a knowledge cutoff of October 2023"; default settings, no browsing/search. Outputs "independently reviewed by participating clinicians and verified by two senior clinical experts."
8. Funding: Emerging Discipline Leader Program (2024-YZ-HBDTR-ZYY-2024; YZ-HBDTR-ZYY-2025) and Wuxi Health Committee Top Talent Support Program (HB2023015).

**NOT SAID**
- **No real patients.** The title and abstract say "**simulated** clinical decision making" / "predefined clinical scenarios". No patient harm was measured and no clinical outcome is reported.
- The number of clinicians, number of centres, number of scenarios and number of hallucinations are **not stated on the page as retrieved** (abstract only). Do not assert a participant count.
- The model tested is GPT-4o accessed in July 2024 — the paper does not claim the finding transfers to current-generation models.

---

## 4. Multi-agent LLM diagnosis — benchmarks vs real ED encounters
**URL:** https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.09.24.26363897
**OPENS:** yes
**PUBLISHED:** "Posted September 26, 2026." (v1) — DOI stamp 2026.09.24. **Note: the repo ran this in the 2026-09-27 edition; the preprint posted 26 September.**
**Title:** "Perspective independence, more than personas, drives LLM teams - and where they reverse"
**Authors:** Jun Feng, Yuhao Jiao, Yiyao Li, Longxin Xie, Wenyu Peng, Xuefeng Sun

**CONFIRMED** (verbatim from abstract)
1. "We compared a single direct call, five personas in one context, and the same five roles as isolated agents integrated by a moderator, with five repeat runs per case, on 87 CPC cases, 406 MedCaseReasoning cases, and 364 emergency department encounters, under an LLM judge validated against clinicians."
2. "On the external benchmark the team beat the single call on both pre-specified recall endpoints (top-3 +3.0 points, p = 0.0079; top-5 +3.9, p = 3.8 x 10^-5;); a factorial attributes the gain to independent generation plus moderated synthesis, not the specialist roles."
3. "On real emergency presentations the benefit reversed (top-1 40.1% versus 34.3%, p < 0.0001), carried by the specialist role lists and surviving added objective results."
4. "Deployment should key on the question and the input at hand."

**NOT SAID**
- Not peer reviewed. The 364 ED encounters are **cases evaluated by an LLM judge**, not a prospective deployment in an ED; no clinician decision, triage outcome or patient outcome was changed or measured. The judge is described only as "validated against clinicians" — no validation statistic is given in the abstract.
- The abstract does not name the underlying model(s) or vendor. It does not claim multi-agent systems are harmful to patients, only that the benchmark gain reverses.

---

## 5. Blue Cross Blue Shield Association — $942M and AI coding
**URL:** https://www.fiercehealthcare.com/finance/hospitals-use-ai-coding-tools-cost-bcbsa-plans-942m-more-similar-care-analysis
**OPENS:** yes (via `scripts/fetch.js`; WebFetch got HTTP 403)
**PUBLISHED:** "**Sep 24, 2026 6:00am**" (no timezone shown). By Dave Muoio. **Note: the repo ran this in the 2026-09-25 edition; the article is dated 24 September.**
**Headline:** "Hospitals' use of AI coding tools cost BCBSA plans $942M more for similar care: analysis"

**CONFIRMED**
1. "the share of medically complex cases billed to its Blue plan members has risen from 37% at the beginning of 2023 to 40% by the end of 2025."
2. "About 70% of the coding intensity increase stems from more than 55,000 more cases from the 2023 baseline in which secondary diagnoses pushed a claim into a higher-severity, higher-reimbursement diagnosis-related group (DRG)."
3. "The increase in coding intensity since baseline translates to an estimated $942 million of additional costs shouldered by BCBSA's member plans over two years, of which $653 million stemmed from secondary diagnoses ($11,000 per excess complex case)."
4. Luke Chalker, senior vice president of product and data science at BCBSA and a co-author: "Critically, what we found is underneath all of that data [was] no change in corresponding care for a more complex patient… We now see that coding has materially changed. We see that. Non-Blues see that—they talk about it sometimes in earnings reports and things like that. But we find no evidence of a corresponding change in care, and that's because the reimbursement mechanisms that exist allow this."
5. Chalker: the $942 million estimate "is purely for [where] we believe there is no change in care delivered," and excludes anything that led to a hospital documenting that it delivered additional care.
6. BCBSA "referenced a June survey in which more than 63% of healthcare organizations reported using AI in their revenue cycle workflows."
7. Major bowel procedures DRG: "claims at the highest level of complexity rose from 10.2% to 22.7% while non-complex cases dipped from 36.6% to 32.8%, together accounting for nearly $61 million of the analysis' incremental claims costs."
8. Clinical-discordance check: top quartile of hospitals for complex DRG cases "had similar or lower treatment intensity (ICU utilization, transfusion, reoperation and median length of stay) than their peers, with 65% of completed DRG cases, per the white paper."
9. Posthemorrhagic anemia ("a common bump code"): top quartile for anemia diagnosis "13.7% versus 9.9% for the remainder" had lower transfusion rates "16.9% versus 19.3%".
10. White paper: "The consistent inverse relationship between diagnosis-based complexity and both aggregate resource utilization and diagnosis-specific procedural intervention is the strongest indicator that coding escalation reflects documentation practice changes rather than actual patient acuity shifts."
11. Razia Hashmi, BCBSA vice president of clinical affairs: "The question that is worth asking is [with] two similarly situated hospitals, treating similar patients, why would one hospital diverge?… There may be an element of correct coding there, but the likelihood that this is technology-enabled upcoding is higher, in my view."
12. Stated limitation: "BCBSA acknowledged that the analysis is limited due to its reliance on claims rather than clinical documentation".

**NOT SAID**
- BCBSA did **not** measure AI use hospital-by-hospital. AI adoption is an inferred/attributed cause ("stem from 'systemic' adoption of AI revenue cycle management tools"); no hospital is named and no tool vendor is named. Hashmi's phrasing is explicitly probabilistic ("the likelihood … is higher, in my view").
- No finding of fraud, no regulatory action, no peer review — this is a payer trade-association white paper, not an independent study. The article gives no hospital-industry rebuttal quote for this specific analysis.

---

## 6. Nature Medicine — Alzheimer's graph neural network (PASCode)
**URL:** https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-04128-1
**OPENS:** yes (via `scripts/fetch.js`)
**PUBLISHED:** Received 26 June 2025 · Accepted 18 November 2025 · **Published: 23 September 2026**. **Note: the repo ran it in the 2026-09-24 edition; published 23 September.**
**Title:** "AI-based characterization of Alzheimer's disease phenotypes from population-scale single-cell data"

**CONFIRMED**
1. "the PsychAD project generated a population-level single-nucleus RNA sequencing dataset comprising over 6 million nuclei from the prefrontal cortex of >1,000 individual brains" — the Main text gives the precise figure: "more than 6.3 million nuclei isolated from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) of **1,494 donors**."
2. Framework name: "Phenotype Associated Single Cell encoder (PASCode)", which "score[s] single-cell phenotype associations".
3. "identified ∼1.5 million phenotype-associated cells (PACs) from **584 donors** with AD-related phenotypes."
4. "PASCode ensembles multiple statistical methods into a graph neural model for robust scoring."
5. "Comparing PACs within **27 brain cell subclasses**, we prioritized cell subpopulations and their expressed genes for various AD phenotypes."
6. Findings listed: microglia subpopulations implicated in AD pathology; reactive astrocyte subtypes "that likely confer cognitive resilience"; "enhanced excitatory/inhibitory imbalance and mitochondrial dysfunction in cognitively impaired AD donors"; astrocytes shared between AD and depression showing "inflammation and endoplasmic reticulum stress pathways".
7. Phenotypes used include Braak stages, Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR), cognitive resilience, and neuropsychiatric symptoms (depression, agitation).
8. "We also validated our findings in external population-scale datasets including AD and major depressive disorder, compiled an AD-phenotypic single-cell atlas and delivered the framework as an open-source tool with pre-trained models and a web application for community use."

**NOT SAID**
- **Post-mortem donor brain tissue, not living patients.** No diagnostic test, no clinical validation, no patient outcome. Causality is explicitly hedged: subpopulations "potentially involved", astrocytes "likely confer" resilience, results "potentially offer valuable insights for precision diagnostic and therapeutic development". No drug target is claimed validated.
- The 1,494 donors are the whole PsychAD cohort; the 1.5 million PACs come from the **584-donor** subset with AD-related phenotype information.

---

## 7. Nature — RetroChimera retrosynthesis
**URL:** https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11160-9
**OPENS:** yes for abstract + metadata; **full text is paywalled** ("This is a preview of subscription content"). Numbers beyond the abstract are not readable.
**PUBLISHED:** Received 26 August 2025 · Accepted 11 September 2026 · **Published: 21 September 2026** (repo ran it 2026-09-22)
**Title:** "Chemist-aligned retrosynthesis by ensembling diverse inductive bias models"
**Authors/institutions:** Krzysztof Maziarz, Guoqing Liu, Felix Pultar (equal contribution), … Christopher M. Bishop, Marwin H. S. Segler — **Microsoft Research AI for Science** (Cambridge, UK); **Novartis Biomedical Research** (Basel); **GSK** (Stevenage); University of Cambridge; Jagiellonian University; Bergische Universität Wuppertal.

**CONFIRMED** (verbatim from abstract)
1. "we analyze the failure modes of current AI models and propose RetroChimera: a frontier retrosynthesis model, built upon two newly developed components with complementary inductive biases, integrated via a novel, learning-based ensembling strategy."
2. "Through experiments across several orders of magnitude in data scale, we show RetroChimera outperforms leading baselines, demonstrating robustness outside the training data, as well as the ability to learn from very small numbers of examples per reaction class."
3. "Using both pairwise and pointwise setups, we find that organic chemists prefer predictions from RetroChimera over published reference reactions and over other AI models."
4. "Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot transfer and fine-tuning on internal datasets from two major pharmaceutical companies, showing robust generalization under distribution shift."

**NOT SAID**
- The abstract gives **no numbers at all** for the chemist-preference study: no number of chemists, no number of routes/reactions judged, no preference percentage, no statistical test. Anything quantitative about "chemists prefer" is behind the paywall and should not be asserted.
- No claim that any predicted route was executed in the laboratory, and no claim of a synthesised molecule, yield or time saving. "Two major pharmaceutical companies" are not named in the abstract (Novartis and GSK appear only as author affiliations).

---

## 8. Preprint — Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 on anesthesiology exam
**URL:** https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.09.21.26363591v1
**OPENS:** yes
**PUBLISHED:** "Posted September 22, 2026." (v1) — DOI stamp 2026.09.21. Repo ran it 2026-09-23.
**Title:** "Assessing the Performance of Artificial Intelligence on Anesthesiology In-Training Examinations and Applicability in Medical Education"
**Authors:** Andrew F. Ibrahim, John F. Zaki

**CONFIRMED** (verbatim from abstract)
1. "A total of 1,001 single-best-answer questions from an anesthesiology ITE review text, spanning 11 content chapters, were administered to Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6. No questions were excluded."
2. "Each item was presented once in a fresh, stateless context with no tool access, retrieval, answer key, or explanation provided in the prompt."
3. "all 27 figure-dependent items were administered with their published figures supplied. Accuracy between models was compared using McNemar's test."
4. "Claude Opus 5 answered 947/1,001 items correctly (94.6%; 95% CI, 93.0–95.8), and GPT-5.6 answered 946/1,001 correctly (94.5%; 95% CI, 92.9–95.8); the difference was not significant (McNemar p=1.00)."
5. "On standard questions, accuracy was 94.3% and 94.6% for Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6, respectively; on the 18 figure-based questions with figures supplied, accuracy was 94.4% and 83.3%, respectively; and both models achieved 100% accuracy on image-option items."
6. "Withholding figures from the same 18 figure-based questions reduced pooled accuracy from 88.9% to 52.8% (exact McNemar p=0.03 and p=0.04 for Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6, respectively)."
7. "The models agreed on 957/1,001 items (95.6%). Of the 33 items both models answered incorrectly, they selected the same incorrect option on 32 (97%)."
8. "placing both models within the highest band of the ITE normative framework, corresponding approximately to the 99th percentile across training levels. By comparison, our prior work with previous models placed ChatGPT-3.5 at the 52nd, 3rd, and 1st percentiles and ChatGPT-4.0 at the 99th, 95th, and 84th percentiles across increasing levels of training."
9. "These findings support an increasingly promising role for LLMs as accessible, on-demand educational adjuncts for anesthesiology trainees, provided complete source material is supplied and outputs are critically reviewed."

**NOT SAID / correction**
- The "collapse without the figures" applies to a **subset of 18 questions**, pooled across both models (88.9% → 52.8%), **not** to the 1,001-question score. The paper does **not** report a per-model figure-withheld accuracy.
- Note the count discrepancy the paper itself carries: "all 27 figure-dependent items" but the figure-based accuracy analysis uses "the 18 figure-based questions" (the remainder being "image-option items").
- No patients, no clinical task, no real workflow. The stated use case is **education** ("educational adjuncts for anesthesiology trainees"), not clinical decision support. The 99th-percentile claim is "approximately" against a normative framework, not against a tested cohort of residents.

---

## 9. TAILORx reanalysis preprint — AI pathology model and chemotherapy benefit
**URL:** https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.09.12.26362500v2
**OPENS:** yes
**PUBLISHED:** **v1 posted September 20, 2026; v2 posted September 22, 2026** (DOI stamp 2026.09.12). Repo ran it 2026-09-23 and cites v2.
**Title:** "An AI Model Identifies Chemotherapy Benefit in Node-Negative HR+/HER2- Breast Cancer Patients from TAILORx, a Phase 3 Randomized Clinical Trial"
**Authors:** Nancy Chan, Cerise Tang, Dhruva Biswas, Jungkyu Park, Ken G. Zeng, Joseph Cappadona, Chuwen Liu, Alec McClean, Jeroen Berrevoets, Linus Bao, Bartosz Machura, Robert J. Gray, Victoria Wang, Jan Witowski, Krzysztof J. Geras, Joseph A. Sparano, TAILORx Investigators

**CONFIRMED** (verbatim from abstract)
1. "We analyzed 6735 patients from the TAILORx trial using Ataraxis Breast CTX with pathology images (H&E slides) and RS available."
2. "CTX is an AI model which integrates morphologic features extracted from H&E-stained slides with clinical variables to generate individualized predictions of prognosis (CTX-prognostic) and chemotherapy benefit (CTX-benefit). No data from TAILORx were used to train CTX and CTX was not retrained or recalibrated for this study. Analyses were prespecified in a protocol approved by ECOG-ACRIN."
3. "Among patients treated with endocrine therapy alone, CTX-prognostic predicted disease-free interval (DFI), with a hazard ratio per 1 SD increase of 1.651 (95% CI, 1.511-1.803, p < 0.001) and C-index of 0.736 (95% CI, 0.697-0.770)."
4. "Performance was similar in patients treated with chemoendocrine therapy (hazard ratio = 1.642 [95% CI, 1.495-1.804, p < 0.001], C-index = 0.720 [95% CI, 0.681-0.756])."
5. "In the intermediate-RS subgroup, the treatment-by-biomarker interaction for CTX-benefit was significant (p = 0.016), with patients identified as high-benefit deriving a **5.6% increase in observed 5-year DFI rates** from the addition of chemotherapy, compared with no detectable benefit in low-benefit patients."
6. "Stratifying the same subgroup by RS at a threshold selecting a similar proportion of patients yielded no significant interaction (p = 0.20)."
7. "Among intermediate-RS patients, CTX-benefit identified who derived clinically meaningful benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy, a population currently not identifiable by the RS alone."
8. Described on the page as "a secondary analysis" using "retrospective, deidentified data".

**NOT SAID**
- Not peer reviewed. The headline "5 points" is **5.6%**, and it is an **observed 5-year DFI rate difference in a subgroup**, not an overall survival benefit and not an overall-cohort effect. No overall survival, no prospective validation, no size of the high-benefit subgroup given in the abstract.
- The analysis is retrospective on stored slides from a completed trial; no patient was treated according to CTX, and the paper does not claim the model is ready for clinical use or approved.
- "Ataraxis Breast CTX" is a commercial model; the abstract does not state author conflicts.

---

## 10. Boehringer Ingelheim / Envisagenics
**URL:** https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/09/22/3366249/0/en/envisagenics-and-boehringer-ingelheim-enter-multi-target-collaboration-…html
**OPENS:** yes
**PUBLISHED:** "**September 22, 2026 08:00 ET**"; dateline "NEW YORK, Sept. 22, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE)". Source: Envisagenics (company press release). Repo ran it 2026-09-23.

**CONFIRMED** (verbatim)
1. "Envisagenics is eligible to receive more than US$1 billion in potential payments, including an upfront payment, research funding, option fees and development, regulatory and commercial milestones, plus royalties on future product sales".
2. "Envisagenics today announced a multi-year research collaboration and option agreement with Boehringer Ingelheim to validate selected tumor-specific targets for the development of first-in-class precision therapies for people living with solid tumors."
3. "Boehringer Ingelheim may apply selected targets across multiple modalities, including antibody-drug conjugates, T-cell engagers and multispecific antibodies."
4. "Upon successful completion of the research program, Boehringer Ingelheim will have the option to exclusively license selected targets for further development and commercialization."
5. Platform: "SpliceCore®", which "combines artificial intelligence, large-scale transcriptomics and experimental validation to identify and prioritize these targets systematically – screening more than **14 million distinct splicing events** to predict disease specificity, patient prevalence and therapeutic suitability."
6. Maria Luisa Pineda, Ph.D., CEO and Co-Founder: "This collaboration validates our vision that alternative RNA splicing represents one of the richest untapped sources of novel disease-specific therapeutic targets across human disease. 3. **Multi-agent LLM preprint (item 4)** — real patient encounters, but retrospectively scored: "**364 emergency department encounters**", "top-1 **40.1% versus 34.3%**, p < 0.0001", judged by "an LLM judge validated against clinicians". No clinician acted on the output.

**Items 4 and 3** are the direct pair; **item 1** supplies a third, quantified version of the same gap.

- **Item 3, npj Digital Medicine (s41746-026-03294-x):**

### 2609.28197

# Title: PASTABench: Proactive Assessment of Sequential Trajectories for Agent Safety
--
Authors: Jiapeng Sun , Yujin Zhou , Han Zhu , Pengcheng Wen , Jiayi Zhou , Sirui Han , Yike Guo
View a PDF of the paper titled PASTABench: Proactive Assessment of Sequential Trajectories for Agent Safety, by Jiapeng Sun and 6 other authors

--
Abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) evolve into autonomous agents that alter real-world states, ensuring operational safety across multi-step workflows has become a critical challenge. While recent work has moved beyond single-turn evaluation toward multi-turn paradigms, key limitations persist: step-level methods treat actions in isolation, missing how risks accumulate, while trajectory-level evaluations operate post-hoc, offering no opportunity for timely intervention. To address these limitations, we formalize Decoupled Proactive Safety Monitoring along three dimensions: whether to intervene, when to intervene, and what the risk is. We introduce PASTABench, a benchmark of 1,139 multi-turn trajectories spanning 5 risk categories and 13 subcategories. We further propose the Optimal Intervention Window (OIW), anchored by annotated Earliest-Signal and Trigger turns, to quantify intervention timeliness. Evaluation of 16 LLMs reveals that proactive intervention remains largely unsolved, with the best model achieving only 40.74% optimal-timing interventions. Fine-grained diagnosis further uncovers pervasive lexical overfitting: competitive safety scores of smaller models mask keyword hypersensitivity rather than genuine risk comprehension, as their proactive capability largely collapses once hazard vocabulary is neutralized.

# Title: Where Cyber Agents Struggle: Bottleneck Analysis of Multi-Stage LLM Agents
--
Authors: Saeedeh Lohrasbi , Mohammad Mamun , Ahmed Yehia , Scott Buffett , Sherif Saad
View a PDF of the paper titled Where Cyber Agents Struggle: Bottleneck Analysis of Multi-Stage LLM Agents, by Saeedeh Lohrasbi and 4 other authors

--
Abstract: Multi-stage LLM-based cyber agents may complete attack workflows while remaining brittle, costly, or reliant on incorrect interpretations of execution evidence. Success rates alone obscure inefficiency, adaptation through retries, and recognition of success or failure. We present an end-to-end diagnostic study of an Autonomous Adversary system with orchestrator, executor, and validator LLMs in enterprise-like lateral-movement scenarios. Six frontier models are evaluated across two scenarios and three modes: expert-defined, self-scaffolded, and fully autonomous. We assess validator consistency and evidence grounding; introduce a subtask-conditioned, cost-aware score for abnormal token use, retries, and runtime; and use comparative LLM-as-a-Judge analysis to identify planning deficiencies, including tool misalignment, plan similarity, over-specification, inadequate probing, and weak recovery. Validators are generally relevant and evidence-grounded but often nonspecific and overly optimistic. Bottlenecks cluster in credential and lateral-movement tasks, spread with scenario complexity, and vary more under full autonomy. Reliable evaluation must assess outcomes, evidence interpretation, resource use, and adaptation after failure.

### 2609.24890
[Submitted on 21 Sep 2026]

# Title: OSWorld-Pro: Process-based Evaluation for Computer Use Agents
--
Authors: Zhilin Wang , Shaokun Zhang , Yifan Zhang , Hao Zhang , Jin Xu , Binfeng Xu , Jian Hu , Yunheng Zou , Karan Sapra , Andrew Tao , Jan Kautz , Yi Dong
View a PDF of the paper titled OSWorld-Pro: Process-based Evaluation for Computer Use Agents, by Zhilin Wang and 11 other authors

--
Abstract: Evaluation of Computer-Use Agents (CUAs) is often limited to the final deliverables they create (at the end of hundreds of steps) and assessed with functional verifiers, as seen in OSWorld. However, such evaluation of end-state performance lacks transparency into how and why agents fail in various tasks, obfuscating critical insight for subsequent improvement. For instance, agents that err during keyboard inputs would require a different mitigation strategy from those that fail to precisely provide click-based inputs on the graphical UI. We introduce OSWorld-Pro: a set of over 300 tasks containing over 2800 subgoals to enable the procedural evaluation of CUAs grounded in over 67,000 human annotations. We use robust human-aligned LLM-Judges to evaluate the fulfillment of OSWorld-Pro subgoals and thereby reveal the progress that models make throughout a series of sequentially dependent subgoals. Our findings reveal that OSWorld-Pro is challenging even for state-of-the-art LLMs, with top performers like Claude Opus 5 achieving only 75.7% vs. 83.4% on OSWorld. Furthermore, we identify critical process-focused failure modes of various models (e.g. subgoal-irrelevant actions and click-based mistakes) to provide insights to improve performance and efficiency of CUAs.

On Friday I gave the closing keynote at the WeAreDevelopers World Congress North America in San Jose. I tied together the key trends from the past year into a chronological exploration of everything that happened in 2026. The video is on YouTube; here are my annotated slides and notes to accompany the talk.

And as an annotated presentation:

#

I'm going to give a lightning tour of everything that has happened so far in 2026. The year isn't over yet!

#

For me, 2026 started a couple of months earlier in November 2025.

#

November saw the release of two important models: Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1.

As is usually the case with new models, these were incremental improvements on the models that came before them.

But every now and then when a model improves, it crosses an invisible line where something that didn't really work starts working.

In this case, the thing that started working was their coding agents. Claude Code had been around since February 2025, Codex was a little younger.

These two new models, when paired with their respective coding agent harnesses, improved from "often make mistakes" to "reliable enough to use on a day-to-day basis".

Before: HENDERSON, KATSAS, and RAO, Circuit Judges. 
Opinion for the Court filed by Circuit Judge KATSAS. 
Dissenting opinion filed by Circuit Judge HENDERSON. 
KATSAS, Circuit Judge:  This case arises from a decision 
by the Department of War to exclude Claude, an artificial-
intelligence product developed by petitioner Anthropic PBC, 
from its supply chain under the Federal Acquisition Supply 
Chain Security Act of 2018.  The Department made this 
decision after Anthropic refused to relax contractual 
prohibitions on the use of Claude for lethal autonomous 
warfare or domestic surveillance.  Anthropic challenges the 
exclusion as arbitrary, unauthorized by the governing statute, 
and unconstitutional. 
We reject these challenges.  The Department had ample 
support for its conclusion that the continued integration of 
Claude into the Department’s information systems, by the 
Department or its contractors, presented a statutorily covered 
national-security risk.  As Anthropic admits, the company 
encodes restrictions into Claude that prevent the model from 
performing tasks that Anthropic wishes to prevent.  On more 
than one occasion, these restrictions have stopped Claude from 
performing tasks requested by government users.  And 
recently, a dispute arose over whether the contractual 
prohibitions barred the use of Claude in an ongoing overseas 
military operation, leaving the Department uncertain whether 
Claude would perform as needed and intended. 
Anthropic’s constitutional claims are also without merit.  
Its due-process claim fails because the Department promptly 
notified the company of the exclusion and its supporting 
rationale, and then gave the company a fair opportunity to 
contest the exclusion.  And Anthropic’s First Amendment

The Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 
2018 authorizes “covered procurement action[s]” to prevent 
agencies from using information technologies that pose a risk 
to national security.  41 U.S.C. § 4713(a).  Such procurement 
actions include barring agency contracts with a particular 
supplier and subcontracts that use the supplier to perform work 
for the agency.  Id. § 4713(k)(4)(A), (B), (D). 
To take a covered procurement action, an agency head 
must first make a written determination that use of the authority 
to take the action “is necessary to protect national security by 
reducing supply chain risk” and that “less intrusive measures 
are not reasonably available” to reduce that risk.  41 U.S.C. 
§ 4713(b)(3)(A), (B).  The determination must also specify the 
class of covered procurement actions the agency may take

# Maven Smart System Usage Doubles to 100K+ Personnel

**Publication Date:** September 22, 2026

## Key Facts

- Pentagon personnel using Palantir's Maven Smart System (MSS) grew from approximately 50,000 in January 2026 to over 100,000 by September 2026
- The expansion coincided with Operation Epic Fury against Iran
- During the 38-day operation, the U.S. military struck 13,000 targets using Maven capabilities

## Officials Quoted

**James Mazol, Deputy Undersecretary of Defense for Research and Engineering:**
> "In January of this year, we had about 50,000 people using Maven. Then [Operation] Epic Fury kicks off, and now we're up to over 100,000"

**Cameron Stanley, Pentagon Chief Digital and AI Officer:**
> "That's data-centric warfare. That's using AI at scale"

## Additional Context

- Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg directed transitioning MSS into a formal program of record by fiscal year end (March 2026 memo)
- Contract ceiling raised to over $1 billion
- Pentagon identifies secure compute capacity as a critical challenge for classified AI training
- The "AI Arsenal" program seeks government-owned, contractor-operated data centers for sovereign compute resources

# Northcom's Next Counter-Drone Demo: Urban Focus

**Publication Date:** September 25, 2026

## Key Facts

U.S. Northern Command will conduct its next Falcon Peak exercise in an urban environment for the first time, marking a significant shift in counter-drone testing strategy.

**Location & Timeline:** The specific city and date haven't been announced. Brig. Gen. Jason "Ox" Rueschhoff stated, "We're working on that," when asked about details.

**Current Exercise:** Falcon Peak 26.2 recently concluded at Yuma Proving Ground, Arizona (September 2026), focusing on the U.S.-Mexico border.

## Strategic Rationale

Rueschhoff emphasized that "Homeland defense is not about protecting from outside, it's also protecting inside." The urban setting introduces new challenges including collateral damage concerns, signal interference from buildings, and radar complications absent in open desert environments.

## Vendors & Technologies

Anduril's autonomous command-and-control platform **Lattice** featured in Falcon Peak 26.2, along with Genesis Arms' Gen-12 SBM counter-drone system.

## Program Background

Northcom initiated Falcon Peak exercises in October 2024 to establish baseline domestic counter-UAS testing procedures. The series progressively evolved from evaluating ready-to-use platforms to operational border defense scenarios.

# Cartel Drone Operations on U.S.-Mexico Border Intensifying

**Publication Date:** September 24, 2026

## Key Facts

- The Joint Task Force-Southern Border (JTF-SB), launched in March 2025, reports that drug cartels are increasingly adapting their drone tactics and technology use
- Military officials declined to disclose specific data on drone threat frequency, payload types, sizes, or proximity for operational security reasons

Lt. Commander Lauren Cole stated that cartels are "evolving in how they use drones, and they're enhancing how they use drones," adding that "they get more creative every day — but so do we."

Cole also warned that criminal organizations use surveillance drones to "monitor the movements and patterns" of U.S. service members and officials.

## Counter-Drone Technologies Deployed

- DroneBuster (handheld electronic detection/disabling device)
- Pitbull drone jammer
- Autonomous command-and-control systems

## Additional Context

The effort supports the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Customs and Border Protection with non-law enforcement assistance, representing a priority under the Trump administration's border security strategy.

# Navy Expanding Sea Drone Marketplace with New MUSV Solicitation

**Publication Date:** September 24, 2026

## Key Facts

The U.S. Navy issued a call for solutions to onboard "Phase II" medium unmanned surface vessels (MUSVs) to its digital marketplace hosted on drones.mil. This effort aims to streamline acquisition of autonomous watercraft for high-volume procurement over the coming decade.

## Program Details

**Name:** Medium Unmanned Surface Vessel (MUSV) marketplace initiative

**Timeline:** Call for solutions posted September 2026; evaluation includes capability assessment, vessel demonstrations from continental U.S. ports, and marketplace qualification

**Vendors Being Sought:** The Navy seeks "interested parties with expertise in innovative solutions to complex problems, vessel construction, autonomy, perception systems, and general maritime experience."

## Technical Requirements

Proposed systems must meet specific operational standards:
- Autonomous operations in open ocean for multi-day missions (minimum 10 days)
- Payload capacity of at least 2x Twenty-foot Equivalent Units weighing 24,000 kg each
- Maximum displacement: 5,000 metric tonnes
- Maximum length: 90 meters
- Platforms must be ready for operational demonstration at submission

## AI/Autonomy Involvement

The initiative emphasizes "open-architecture autonomy compatibility" and uses "modular design principles" to create adaptable solutions. Evaluation criteria specifically include "open-architecture autonomy compatibility" and rapid-production scalability.

## Strategic Context

This effort supports Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle's "Hedge Strategy," which identifies medium USVs for "scouting, screening, and striking" roles.

112-
113-EFF sued the government back in March for information about the Wasteful and Inappropriate Service Reduction (WISeR) model , a new Medicare program that uses AI to evaluate prior authorization requests for certain medical services. Today, we’re releasing approximately 1,000 pages of records obtained from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) through this litigation, including contracts with tech companies, internal status reports and providers’ complaints about the program. The documents (available here ) show that WISeR has resulted in widespread delays and denials of care, operational chaos, and reports of patient harm.
114-
115-# Why We Sued for Records about WISeR
116-
117:EFF filed the FOIA lawsuit to gain badly needed transparency into an experimental AI program that could jeopardize Medicare beneficiaries' access to care. In January 2026, CMS launched the WISeR model, subjecting seniors in six states to AI-driven prior authorization decisions. Medical providers must now request permission before delivering certain medical treatments if they want assurance that Medicare will cover them. Private companies contracted by CMS evaluate the requests using AI. In the absence of rigorous safeguards, AI-driven prior authorization determinations can lead to unwarranted—and even discriminatory—delays or denials of necessary medical care.
118-
119-Little is known about the AI systems that WISeR vendors are using to process prior authorization requests. Although CMS says that a qualified human clinician must review all denials, research has shown that AI-generated recommendations often influence human decisions. And the design of the WISeR program creates a financial incentive for vendors to deny care, since they are paid for averted expenditures. Just months after the program launched, medical providers reported improper denials, administrative friction, and lengthy delays that have left patients waiting in pain .

HTTP 200 · https://breakingdefense.com/2026/09/dc-circuit-panel-upholds-pentagons-ban-on-anthropic-so-what-comes-next/ · text/html
DC Circuit panel upholds Pentagon’s ban on Anthropic - so what comes next? - Breaking Defense









The Anthropic AI logo appears on a smartphone screen and as the background on a laptop computer screen in this photo illustration in Athens, Greece, on February 24, 2026. (Photo by Nikolas Kokovlis/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

WASHINGTON — Today’s ruling by a three-judge appeals panel against Anthropic in the AI titan’s lawsuit against the Department of Defense is far from the end of the saga, legal experts told Breaking Defense, with Anthropic’s options including further appeals.

The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia today upheld the Pentagon’s controversial designation of the company’s products as a “supply chain risk” to national security. That decision allows the Pentagon to ban all use of Anthropic AI, not only by its own personnel, but also by private sector employees actively working on defense contracts .

However, today’s ruling does not impact a separate and parallel lawsuit in the Northern District of California, where Judge Rita Lin ruled last month against the Trump administration’s attempt to ban Anthropic from all federal contracts. The DC court ruling, by contrast, only covers the Defense Department ban.

Pentagon CTO Emil Michael, who has led the charge against Anthropic, took to social media to declare that “the hammer of justice has smashed AnthropicAI[’s] arguments. They are a Supply Chain Risk to the defense industrial base [and] warfighters will sleep better knowing that no private company will insert their opinions in the chain of command.”

Anthropic, for its part, released a statement that kept its options open. “We respectfully disagree with the court’s decision. Another federal court has already held the government’s parallel designation unlawful,” the statement said, referring to the California case. “We remain confident in our position and are considering all options, including further review.”

“The Department had ample support for its conclusion that the continued integration of Claude into the Department’s information systems, by the Department or its contractors, presented a statutorily covered national-security risk,” Judge Gregory Katsas wrote for himself and Judge Naomi Rao , both Trump appointees. “As Anthropic admits, the company encodes restrictions into Claude that prevent the model from performing tasks that Anthropic wishes to prevent. On more than one occasion, these restrictions have stopped Claude from performing tasks requested by government users.”

“I cannot agree that this is the scenario the Congress had in mind when it enacted FASCSA,” the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018, dissented Judge Karen Henderson , an appointee of George H.W. Bush. That Act was explicitly passed to protect against sabotage by malignant foreign powers, she wrote, not a US company openly building safety and ethics guardrails into its products.

“Because of the law that was used to declare them a supply chain risk, the case went straight to the DC Circuit, which is an appellate court,” Charlie Bullock of the Institute for Law & AI explained to Breaking Defense in an exchange on X.com . “The only appeal from there is to the Supreme Court (which doesn’t have to accept appeals; it exercises discretion and generally grants only a small percentage of appeal requests) or to an en banc panel of the D.C. Circuit (also discretionary, also not granted super often).”

However, “if a full panel is granted, all bets are off,” said Sean Timmons , a former JAG Corps officer now at law firm Tully Rinckey.

The reason, Timmons said, is that the full DC Circuit Court of Appeals has a mix of Trump, Biden, Obama, and Bush appointees. That makes it much more diverse and unpredictable than the randomly selected three-judge panel that issued today’s ruling, which happened to include two Trump appointees.

“You’ve got two people appointed by Trump [saying] we’re not going to step in and undo a decision based on national security parameters, because national security is the sole prerogative of the chief executive,” Timmons told Breaking Defense. “It’s pretty egregious… but when you invoke national security, the courts are kind of like Pontius Pilate: They just want to wash their hands and walk away.”

However, he went on, the Anthropic case is so high profile and so controversial in the legal community that the full court might feel compelled, not only to grant an appeal, but to overturn the panel’s 2-1 ruling. And if any legal team can make that happen, he added, it’s the one Anthropic has assembled.

Bullock independently arrived at a similar conclusion in his analysis online of the 2-1 panel ruling and further prospects. “This was the expected outcome, given the terrible luck Anthropic had with the panel draw,” he posted . “I would expect Anthropic to win before an en banc DC Circuit and likely even before SCOTUS, but they’re not guaranteed any appeal at all.”

## GROUP 1 — Trump–Xi state visit and the US–China AI channel

### 1. White House fact sheet
URL: https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/09/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-advances-a-fair-and-reciprocal-relationship-with-china-while-hosting-historic-state-visit/
OPENS: yes
PUBLISHED: "September 25, 2026" (date only; no time, no timezone shown)
CONFIRMED:
1. Title: "Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Advances a Fair and Reciprocal Relationship with China While Hosting Historic State Visit".
2. Under the heading "MAKING THE WORLD SAFER FOR AMERICANS", two AI bullets, verbatim and in this order:
   - "The two leaders agreed to use the term "super intelligence" rather than "artificial intelligence" to describe the applicable emerging technologies."
   - "The two countries established the U.S.-China Super Intelligence (SI) Dialogue to exchange views on risks and benefits related to SI. The next exchange will occur by November 2026. The United States and China also agreed to establish a bilateral communication channel for SI incidents."
3. Same section: "The two countries agreed to build a constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity."; "The two countries will support each other as respective hosts of G20 and APEC, with both leaders intending to attend each other's Summit."; leaders "discussed on-going global concerns, including Russia, North Korea, and Iran. They agreed that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon and that no country or institution can be allowed to impose tolls on international waterways."; "The two leaders recalled that United States and China were allies in World War II and fought side by side to win the war."; "The President advocated for trilateral arms control negotiations between the United States, Russia, and China."
4. "OPERATIONALIZING THE BOARDS OF TRADE AND INVESTMENT: This week, the two leaders operationalized the cornerstone government-to-government mechanisms of the U.S.-China Board of Trade and the U.S.-China Board of Investment, which were chartered during the May 2026 Summit in Beijing."
5. "Following President Trump's revival of the U.S. coal industry, China will import at least 10 million metric tons of coal from the United States in 2027 and again 2028."
6. "The United States and China continue to work on U.S. concerns regarding supply chain shortages related to rare earths and other critical minerals, with the goal of ensuring shipment levels return to appropriate levels."
7. "In August 2026, acting on information from U.S. law enforcement, China arrested 21 Chinese citizens for the manufacture and distribution of precursor chemicals to illicit drug producers in North America. The United States strongly encouraged maximum sentences, including the death penalty where applicable."
NOT SAID:
- The fact sheet never uses the words "AI safety", "safety channel", "guardrails", "hotline", or "frontier models".
- It does NOT say the next exchange will be in Shenzhen, and gives no venue.
- It says "by November 2026" — not "in November 2026".
- No mention of export controls, chips, semiconductors, Nvidia, or any chip-related AI commitment.
- No mention of Anthropic, the Pentagon designation, or any US domestic AI policy.
- No mention of the $30 billion tariff figure in the AI context (the trade items are separate bullets).

# ANSWERS

## Q1 — The D.C. Circuit opinion, from the opinion itself

**Case name:** *Anthropic PBC, Petitioner v. United States Department of War and Peter B. Hegseth, in his official capacity as Secretary of War, Respondents.* (Note: the caption reads "Peter B. Hegseth"; press accounts call him Pete Hegseth.)

**Docket:** "No. 26-1049", "Consolidated with 26-1162". Posture: "On Petitions for Review of an Agency Action of the Department of War."

**Dates:** "Argued May 19, 2026    Decided September 25, 2026."

**Panel:** "Before: HENDERSON, KATSAS, and RAO, Circuit Judges."

**Authorship and vote:** "Opinion for the Court filed by Circuit Judge KATSAS. / Dissenting opinion filed by Circuit Judge HENDERSON." The opinion itself states no vote count; it is **2–1** by arithmetic (Katsas writing, Rao on the panel with no separate writing, Henderson dissenting). CNBC and Courthouse News both report "2-1" and both state Rao joined Katsas.

**Legal question decided:** Whether the Secretary of War lawfully excluded Anthropic's Claude from the Department's supply chain under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018, 41 U.S.C. § 4713 — specifically the three statutory determinations, plus due-process and First Amendment challenges. In the court's words:

> "This case arises from a decision by the Department of War to exclude Claude, an artificial-intelligence product developed by petitioner Anthropic PBC, from its supply chain under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018. The Department made this decision after Anthropic refused to relax contractual prohibitions on the use of Claude for lethal autonomous warfare or domestic surveillance. Anthropic challenges the exclusion as arbitrary, unauthorized by the governing statute, and unconstitutional."

> "Anthropic challenges each of the Secretary's three key determinations under the Supply Chain Security Act, namely that (A) removing Claude from the Department's supply chain was 'necessary to protect national security by reducing supply chain risk,' 41 U.S.C. § 4713(b)(3)(A); (B) 'less intrusive measures' for reducing that risk were 'not reasonably available,' id. § 4713(b)(3)(B); and (C) an 'urgent national security interest' required 'the immediate exercise' of the removal authority, id. § 4713(c)."

The statutory-interpretation crux, per the dissent (undisputed by the majority): "whether Anthropic qualifies under this definition depends entirely on the scope of section 4713(k)(6)'s residual clause: 'or otherwise manipulate.'"

**Standard of review** (quoting the opinion):

> "These claims are governed by the standards of review set forth in the Supply Chain Security Act, which requires us to 'hold unlawful' covered procurement actions under section 4713 that we find to be 'arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law.' 41 U.S.C. § 1327(b)(2), (2)(A). These standards closely track those in the Administrative Procedure Act. See 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)."

> "On review for arbitrariness, we require only that agency action be 'reasonable and reasonably explained.' FCC v. Prometheus Radio Project, 592 U.S. 414, 423 (2021). Judicial review under this standard is 'deferential,' and this Court may not 'substitute its own policy judgment for that of the agency.'"

> "We review de novo agency determinations on purely legal questions of statutory construction. Loper Bright Enters. v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 412 (2024). In construing statutes implicating national security, we resolve ambiguities against intruding on the national-security determinations of the Executive Branch. See, e.g., Dep't of Navy v. Egan, 484 U.S. 518, 530 (1988)..."

> "Where the application of a statutory term turns primarily on factual determinations, we review the agency's assessment deferentially. Seven County Infrastructure Coal. v. Eagle County, 605 U.S. 168, 181 (2025). And where a factual question turns on assessments of national security, we give the agency more deference, even if constitutional claims are at issue."

**Sentences describing the Pentagon's reasons for the designation** (quoted):

> "The Secretary reasonably concluded that removing Anthropic from the Department's supply chain was necessary to protect national security by reducing supply chain risk to the Department's information systems. Specifically, the Secretary credited a joint recommendation from two senior Department officials that Claude might be 'subject to manipulation' by Anthropic 'in such a manner as to inhibit the DoW's use thereof.' App. 178. Likewise, he credited Under Secretary Michael's conclusion that Anthropic might 'manipulat[e]' the 'design, integrity, and operation' of the Department's Claude models, potentially causing 'critical defense system[s] failing to engage' as intended by the Department. Id. at 182."

> "The determination rested on a recommendation from senior agency officials, which in turn rested on a memorandum from Emil Michael, the Department's Under Secretary for Research and Engineering. Among other things, Michael cited Anthropic's refusal to allow all lawful uses of Claude, its ability to 'alter system guardrails and model weights' governing how Claude responds to user prompts, and its questioning the Department's use of Claude in a sensitive military mission abroad."

> "First, the Secretary determined that use of Claude in Department systems 'presents a significant supply chain risk' and that removing Claude from them was 'necessary to protect national security' by reducing that risk. App. 177. Next, he determined that no 'less intrusive measures' for reducing the risk were 'reasonably available.' Id. Finally, he determined that an 'urgent national security interest' required immediate action."

> "In sum, the Department reasonably feared that Anthropic might manipulate Claude's design to prevent it from performing national-security functions that the Department deems contractually authorized and necessary."

> "Because Anthropic was willing and able to enforce contractual restrictions through model training, the Department reasonably worried that 'critical defense system[s]' supported by Claude might 'fail[] to engage' as the Department would expect."

**The holding, in the court's own summary and conclusion:**

> "We reject these challenges. The Department had ample support for its conclusion that the continued integration of Claude into the Department's information systems, by the Department or its contractors, presented a statutorily covered national-security risk. As Anthropic admits, the company encodes restrictions into Claude that prevent the model from performing tasks that Anthropic wishes to prevent. On more than one occasion, these restrictions have stopped Claude from performing tasks requested by government users. And recently, a dispute arose over whether the contractual prohibitions barred the use of Claude in an ongoing overseas military operation, leaving the Department uncertain whether Claude would perform as needed and intended."

> "Anthropic's constitutional claims are also without merit. Its due-process claim fails because the Department promptly notified the company of the exclusion and its supporting rationale, and then gave the company a fair opportunity to contest the exclusion. And Anthropic's First Amendment claim fails because the Department excluded Anthropic from its supply chain based on the company's refusal to assent to a contract term that the Department deemed essential, not based on the company's support for greater governmental regulation of AI technology."

> "This case raises profoundly difficult questions about the appropriate military uses of an almost unimaginably powerful new technology. The Secretary raises the deeply sobering prospect of overly constrained AI models shutting down unexpectedly and thus causing important military operations to fail. Anthropic raises the deeply sobering prospect of unconstrained AI models hallucinating inappropriate targets for lethal military force. Both possibilities present obvious national-security concerns. But in our Republic, it is the President and the Secretary of War who must determine how best to balance the competing risks. In doing so here, the Secretary did not transgress any limits on his authority under the Supply Chain Security Act or the Constitution. Accordingly, we deny the petitions for review. So ordered."

**Henderson's dissent, key sentences:**

> "Whether the Secretary of the Department of War (Secretary) lawfully invoked his statutory powers under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018 (FASCSA) turns on whether Anthropic falls within the statute's definition of a 'supply chain risk.'"

> "According to Anthropic, the residual clause uses 'manipulate' to denote intentionally subversive acts, carried out through deceptive means. ... The Secretary argues, and the majority agrees, that the term encompasses much more."

> "The Department here made good on its promise to designate Anthropic a supply chain risk after Anthropic declined the Secretary's ultimatum to replace its use restrictions on Claude with a general provision permitting 'all lawful uses.' But suppose the Secretary tells Anthropic's presumed replacement to change its AI-use policies to permit any 'functions that the Department deems necessary' or it will share the same fate as Anthropic. According to today's decision, that contractor will have a choice: Agree to the Secretary's demands or risk being designated a national security threat under FASCSA."

> "[I]t refutes the view that 'manipulat[ion]' of a covered article encompasses anything like the conduct that, under today's holding, gives rise to a supply chain risk—that is, a contractor's honest and upfront enforcement of restrictions on a covered article's use disfavored by the government."

> "For the foregoing reasons, I respectfully dissent."

## Q2 — Does the opinion mention GenAI.mil, the Maven Smart System, or Claude's replacement by other models?

**GenAI.mil: NO.** A case-insensitive search of the full 51-page text for "genai", "gen ai" and "GenAI.mil" returns zero hits. The platform is never named.

**Maven / Maven Smart System: NO.** Zero hits for "maven" or "smart system". Palantir *is* mentioned, but only as an Anthropic customer/contractor subject to Anthropic's use restrictions: "Among other things, it prohibits Palantir from using Claude to…", and in the record description of Amodei's letter to employees that "the Department, OpenAI, and Palantir had not established adequate safety protocols for the use of AI."

**Replacement of Claude by other models: only three passing references, none describing an actual replacement programme.**
1. In the factual background: "The Department quickly moved to expand its contractual relationship with OpenAI, another company that provides AI services." (App. 220.)
2. From the record, Amodei's own words before the designation: he "pledged a 'smooth transition to another provider' '[s]hould the Department choose to offboard Anthropic.'"
3. In Henderson's dissent, as a hypothetical, not a finding: "suppose the Secretary tells Anthropic's presumed replacement to change its AI-use policies to permit any 'functions that the Department deems necessary' or it will share the same fate as Anthropic."

Gemini, Grok, ChatGPT and xAI appear nowhere in the opinion. **Any link between this ruling and the GenAI.mil user figures or the Maven Smart System is a connection the court does not make.** The GenAI.mil link comes from CNBC's reporting ("as the company began negotiating Claude's deployment on the DOD's GenAI.mil AI platform that September, talks collapsed") and must be sourced to CNBC.

## Q3 — How each readout names and describes the AI mechanism, side by side

| | **White House fact sheet** (Sept. 25, 2026) | **Chinese MFA readout** (Updated Sept. 26, 2026 18:16) |
|---|---|---|
| Terminology bullet | "The two leaders agreed to use the term "super intelligence" rather than "artificial intelligence" to describe the applicable emerging technologies." | *(no equivalent — the phrase "super intelligence" does not appear anywhere in the Chinese text)* |
| Mechanism | "The two countries **established** the **U.S.-China Super Intelligence (SI) Dialogue** to exchange views on risks and benefits related to **SI**." | "The two sides **agree on the establishment of** the **China-U.S. AI Dialogue** to exchange views on risks and benefits related to **AI**." |
| Timing | "The next exchange will occur **by** November 2026." | "The next exchange will occur **in** November 2026." |
| Incident channel | "The United States and China also agreed to establish a bilateral communication channel for **SI incidents**." | "China and the U.S. also agree to establish a bilateral communication channel for **AI incidents**." |
| Placement | A bullet inside "MAKING THE WORLD SAFER FOR AMERICANS", alongside Russia/North Korea/Iran, WWII, and trilateral arms control. | Numbered item **7 of 8** "deliverables and understandings", between counter-narcotics (6) and pandas (8). |

**Every difference in wording:**
1. **The technology term.** US: "Super Intelligence (SI)" throughout. China: "AI" throughout. The Chinese text never uses "super intelligence" or "SI", and does not record any agreement on terminology — even though the US fact sheet says "the two leaders agreed" to it.
2. **Country order in the title of the mechanism.** "U.S.-China Super Intelligence (SI) Dialogue" vs. "China-U.S. AI Dialogue" — each side puts itself first, so the two documents do not name the same body identically in any respect.
3. **Verb and tense.** US: "established" (completed act). China: "agree on the establishment of" (agreement to establish). The US text asserts the body exists; the Chinese text asserts consent to create it.
4. **"by" vs "in" November 2026.** The US sets an outside deadline; China states a month.
5. **Everything else is near-identical**, including the shared formula "to exchange views on risks and benefits related to [SI/AI]" and "bilateral communication channel for [SI/AI] incidents" — the two readouts are plainly drafted from one agreed text with the technology term and country order swapped.
6. **Neither readout** names a venue, a participant list, a chair, a secretariat, an escalation threshold, a definition of "incident", or any safety commitment. Bessent's separate CNBC account (Sept. 21) adds a third name, "the USA-China AI dialogues", and a venue neither readout gives, "probably in two months in Shenzhen".

## Q4 — What the Washington Post (via Spokesman-Review) says was removed from the UN draft

**What was removed** (verbatim from the article):

> "They stripped language requiring the systems to operate in a 'predictable' and 'reliable' manner, the people said, and removed a clause mandating that ethical considerations be taken into account when using AI weaponry. The U.S. and Russian teams also removed a provision requiring that humans review military targets developed by AI before a strike, they added."

**By whom:** "U.S. and Russian diplomats". The article gives no names. It describes the method:

> "In a closed-door session, with U.N. cameras turned off and civil society observers removed, Washington and Moscow deployed their army of about 10 lawyers each – nearly twice the diplomatic presence of other delegations – to make changes that moved so quickly that the smaller delegations were left dizzied, the three people said."
> "'It was death by a thousand paper cuts,' said one of the people."

**Sourcing:** "according to three people familiar with the negotiations, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive closed-door proceedings, and documents reviewed by the Washington Post." "The U.S. State Department, the Russian Foreign Ministry and the United Nations did not return requests for comment." The article states "the details of which are previously unreported."

**When:** "Early this month" / "at the talks in Geneva in early September" — on "the last day of negotiations", over "the next roughly 15 hours". The article gives **no specific calendar date**. Location: "a cavernous U.N. conference room in Switzerland".

**What stage the draft is at** (verbatim):

> "The lethal autonomous weapons negotiations in the U.N. are currently nonbinding, though the talks could open the door to a landmark treaty that is legally binding if member nations agree. It presents the most advanced global effort to regulate how AI weapons are used in the battlefield."

> "In November, nations will come together in Geneva to discuss whether talks can turn into an official mandate or potentially a legally binding treaty."

Earlier framing: diplomats were "working toward a muscular treaty to regulate the use of lethal autonomous weapons – the first agreement governing the use of killer artificial intelligence arms", and "the latest directive is the furthest the effort has advanced." Nicole van Rooijen (Stop Killer Robots) notes the talks "require dozens of nations to reach consensus", and that the US and Russia "have the power to block any significant progress that is made by the vast majority of states who do want to move forward on a binding treaty."

**NOT said:** the piece never gives the draft's formal title or the body's official name (CCW/GGE is not named), never dates the session precisely, never names a diplomat on either side, and does not say the text was adopted, rejected or finalised — only that provisions were removed from a nonbinding draft that will be revisited in Geneva in November.

# CROSS-CUTTING CAUTIONS FOR THE EDIT

1. **No CNBC article in this set displays a publication date or time** on the page or in metadata. Only the URL path gives a date. If the briefing states CNBC timestamps, they are not sourced from the pages.
2. **The D.C. Circuit opinion contains no order delaying its effect.** CNBC alone reports the panel would delay it; the PDF ends flatly at "So ordered."
3. **The opinion never mentions GenAI.mil or Maven.** Do not let the Group 2 and Group 3 stories be woven into a single causal chain that no source draws.
4. **Three different names exist for the same US–China mechanism** — "U.S.-China Super Intelligence (SI) Dialogue" (White House), "China-U.S. AI Dialogue" (MFA), "the USA-China AI dialogues" (Bessent on CNBC). Pick one and attribute it.
5. **GenAI.mil user figures conflict** between Defense One (over 2 million weekly logins, with 1.7m described as a July figure) and DefenseScoop (1.7 million of 3 million cumulative, ~500,000 daily). They measure different things and were said by different officials on different days.
6. **Trump's "leading by at least a year, maybe a year and a half"** line does not appear in the PBS article text. The verified Trump quotes on US lead are the ones given under items 3 and 4 above.
7. **Crypto Briefing dates DeepSeek's R1 public release to March 2026**, which appears to be an error; the piece is pure aggregation of a Bloomberg report published the same day.
8. Anthropic's parallel win is *Anthropic PBC v. U.S. Dep't of War*, No. 26-cv-01996 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 27, 2026), under **10 U.S.C. § 3252** — a different and, per the D.C. Circuit, "much narrower" statute than 41 U.S.C. § 4713. The D.C. Circuit expressly accepted the Northern District's finding that Anthropic acted with no bad motive, and held bad motive is not required under § 4713.
